Clarifying the Miscellaneous Rituals and Deportment of the Various Schools. I. The Origins of the Precepts (*Vinaya-nidāna*). The first [section]: The Great Sage, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings, [established the precepts].
He manifested birth beneath the King of Trees in the Kāpiśī forest and attained enlightenment;
for forty-nine years, he transformed sentient beings according to their conditions.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he entrusted this Vinaya Piṭaka to Upāli.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa presided over the Three Jewels and selected five hundred great arhats who, in the city of Rājagṛha, compiled the Tripiṭaka.
At that time, during a single summer retreat, Upāli ascended the high seat eighty times and fully recited the Mahāvibhaṅga;
thus there were eighty recitations.
He entrusted them all to Mahākāśyapa.
When Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he in turn entrusted the Vinaya Piṭaka to Ānanda.
As Ānanda was approaching his passing, he entrusted [the Dharma] to two great beings:
the first named Śāṇakavāsin and the second named Madhyāntika. This is according to the account in the *Dharmaguptaka-dharmagaṇḍī-śāstra* (The Scripture on the Entrustment of the Dharma-treasury).
Madhyāntika traveled to Kaśmīra to propagate the Dharma;
this is not further recorded in the sūtras.
Śāṇakavāsin propagated the Dharma while residing in Rājagṛha.
At the time of his passing, he entrusted the Dharma to Upagupta.
From Upagupta upwards, there were five great masters,
all of whom fully mastered the eighty thousand treasuries of the Dharma.
His wisdom and eloquence surpassed all others.
Although Upagupta had attained dharanis and supernormal powers, no one could compare to him in the power of his wisdom.
Upagupta had five disciples.
First is the Sarvāstivāda,
the masters of which are the compilers of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Second is the Mahīśāsaka.
This person's name is Fǎzhèng;
he possesses the spiritual capacity for the Mahāyāna and is the master of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The third was Miśa-sai (Miśraka),
who was the master of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya).
The fourth was Vātsīputra.
This is the master of the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya.
Fifth is the Kāśyapīya;
this [school] does not yet exist in this land.
These five individuals were all great arhats;
however, they were unable to maintain the entire treasury of the eighty thousand dharmas in its entirety.
Consequently, each followed their own perspective and thus divided [the teachings] into five schools.
Śākyamuni appeared in this land during the time of King You of the Zhou dynasty;
it was not until the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han that the scriptures and images first arrived,
and it took nearly a hundred years before there were even bhikṣus.
Zhi Qian and Zhu Foshuo had a slight understanding of the Chinese language;
they translated Indic scriptures at an early stage.
This continued until Yao Xing, the ruler of the Qin, developed deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.
In the eighth year of the Hongshi era,
at Caotang Monastery in Chang’an,
he invited the Indian śramaṇa Master Kumārajīva to retranslate it.
The former Dharma Master Shi was skilled in understanding foreign languages and possessed clear comprehension of the Buddha-dharma;
thus, the Buddha-dharma spread widely. [This is recorded in] the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
In the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty,
there was a Tripitaka Master from the kingdom of Kaśmīra named Puṇyatāra.
Having received and upheld the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, he arrived at Chang'an and,
together with Dharma Master Kumārajīva, translated it;
however, one portion remained unfinished.
When the Tripitaka Master passed away,
the Dharma Master Yuan of Lushan continued the translation together with Dharmaruci.
Later, there was another Vinaya Master of the Tripiṭaka named Vimalākṣa,
who had been a teacher under whom Kumārajīva had studied; he arrived here in person.
At Shijian Temple in Shouchun, the Vinaya texts were re-edited;
three additional fascicles were produced,
while the preface to the Vinaya was set aside.
Subsequently, the Vinaya flourished in this land.
First was the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, then the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.
There was also the Śramaṇa Zhifaling of the Jin state.
Having personally traveled to the kingdom of Khotan and obtained the Indic manuscript, he returned to the kingdom of Qin.
In the twelfth year of Hongshi, the ruler of Qin, Yao Chang,
assembled three hundred śramaṇas of eminent virtue at Zhongxing Temple in Chang’an.
He invited the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra named Buddhayaśas, a Mahāyāna Vinaya Master,
to translate the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The monk Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou acted as the oral interpreter.
Hu protected [the teachings] for the Han.
Pen-receivers included Daoyun and others of the Qin state.
This is the second part of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* as it flowed eastward.
The third is the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
There was a Tripitaka Master from Kaśmīra named Daśabala.
The five-fascicle Hu-language manuscript was brought to Yangzhou.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Jingping era of the Jin dynasty,
the Jin Court Attendant (Shizhong) Wang Silian of Langye, together with the bhikṣu Zhu Daosheng and others, requested that it be translated.
The Prevalence of the Vinaya, Part Three of the Five Divisions: The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya.
There was a bhikṣu from this land named Faxian, who held his body in light regard and the Dharma in high esteem.
He traveled in person to the Hu country to seek out sūtras and śāstras, arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Magadha. There,
he transcribed the Hu (Sanskrit) original at the Deva Temple south of the Aśoka Stūpa.
He was about to return to this country.
On the eleventh month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he arrived in Yangzhou.
At Douchang Temple, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra, he translated the Nirvāṇa Sūtra in six fascicles.

This is the fourth section on the emergence of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in this land. The *Kāśyapīya-vinaya*, also known as the *Kāśyapīya* school’s single-part vinaya, does not circulate in this land because sentient beings have not yet generated the conditions for its appearance.

2. The Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries Clarify the Method for Receiving Precepts; Chapter Twenty of the Recitation: The Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries Clarify the Method for Receiving Precepts. This section clarifies ten methods for receiving precepts.
First, the spontaneous attainment of precepts,
which refers to the Buddha’s self-awakening without a teacher;
second, the attainment of precepts through one's own nature.
This refers to Mahākāśyapa,
who attained the precepts through the realization of the Truths (dṛṣṭisatyaprāpta).
It also refers to the five bhikṣus, including Aśvajit and others, who, upon hearing the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, immediately attained full ordination.
Fourth is receiving the precepts through the "Come, monk" (ehi-bhikṣu) formula.
This refers to Yaśas and others, as well as those ordained by the Tathāgata throughout his entire lifetime through the "Come, monk" formula. Why is this so?
The Buddha, the Dharma King, personally conferred the precepts upon them;
these were their final bodies.
As bhikṣus, they never again studied the impermanence of the earth.
There are five ways of obtaining the precepts through the threefold formula;
that is to say, prior to the establishment of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual),
those ordained by Arhats obtained full ordination (*upasampadā*) merely by receiving the Three Refuges.
Sixth, the attainment of precepts through question and answer,
also known as *abhidharma-discourse*.
This refers to the novice Śrāmaṇera Sudāya, who was only seven years old at the time.
The Buddha questioned him on the meaning of these points,
and he answered each one.
The Buddha, approving of his responses as being in accord with the noble mind, commanded the bhikṣus to confer full ordination upon him.
One obtains the precepts through question and answer;
because it was due to an injunction to the bhikṣus, it is also called "obtaining the precepts through an injunction and listening.
Seventh, obtaining the precepts through the Eight Respectful Rules.
It is also called the eight heavy rules;
it is also called the Dharma of the Venerable Teacher;
it is also called the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed.
This refers to Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred Śākya women who sought ordination from the Buddha.
The Buddha sent Ānanda to grant them the Eight Respectful Rules; having heard and accepted them, they were ordained.
They were named after these Eight Respectful Rules.

Therefore, it is said that she obtained the precepts through the Eight Rules of Respect. The *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states: "After Mahāprajāpatī heard the eight dharmas from Ānanda, she received them with joy and reverence.
She then said to Ānanda, 'Please inform the Buddha on my behalf.'"
Among these eight matters, she further made a request:
"I pray that you will permit bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to bhikṣus according to their seniority.
How can a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old pay homage to a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If I were to permit bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to bhikṣus according to their seniority,
such a thing would be impossible."
Having heard this, Ānanda returned and reported it.
Mahāprajāpatī spoke again:
"Receive it upon the crown of your head with reverence."
The Buddha said,
"Mahāprajāpatī, rejoice and practice accordingly.
By these eight rules, one is permitted to be called 'one who has gone forth' and to receive full ordination."
She spoke again to Ānanda,
"What now shall become of these five hundred Śākya women?
Please speak to the Buddha on my behalf once more."
The Buddha said,
"I permit Mahāprajāpatī to act as her preceptor;
she shall receive the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations) within an assembly of ten bhikṣus."
At one time, a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) may involve three persons but not four.
Thus, it was that Āṣāḍhā alone received the eight weighty precepts (*gurudharma*),
while the five hundred Śākya women received the full ordination through the *karmavācanā*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is also like this.
If one follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
the five hundred Śākya women also received the precepts by means of the eight respectful rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
Eighth is receiving the precepts by means of a messenger.
This refers to the case of the courtesan Upacālā, whose countenance was so exceptionally beautiful that whenever she left the monastery,
it would create obstacles leading to the violation of her conduct.
The Noble One granted permission for one bhikṣuṇī to be dispatched as a messenger to the great Saṃgha to receive the precepts on her behalf; therefore,
this is called "receiving the precepts by means of a messenger."
Receiving the precepts through the ninefold *karmavācanā* refers to the formal procedure performed by a quorum of ten monks.
In border regions, the full ordination may be received from a group of five who maintain the Vinaya.
Because the Buddha-dharma was first being practiced in a frontier region,
the monastic community was sparse and difficult to assemble.
The Great Sage granted permission for the five men to receive the precepts.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Those who have attained arhatship..."
This is called going forth and receiving the full precepts.
This person attains the supreme Dharma;
it is called receiving the precepts through the supreme Dharma.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
At one time, there was a person less than twenty years of age who received full ordination;
subsequently, harboring doubts, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to count the months in the womb as well as the months of conception; yet even with these, they are still not full.
The Buddha said.
"Does this person attain arhatship?
He replied, "He does."
The Buddha said,
"This person is called one who has received the full ordination (upasampadā) in the highest manner.
Furthermore, among the community of nuns, a woman who was previously married and is twelve years of age may be permitted to receive the full precepts."
In total, there are twelve ways of receiving the precepts.
Among these twelve, the spontaneous attainment of the precepts occurs only for the Buddha alone;
the attainment of the precepts through self-vow likewise occurs only for the Buddha alone.
Only Mahākāśyapa alone attained the precepts through the realization of the Truths,
which was restricted to the village of Kuṇḍala;
the five [bhikṣus] attained the precepts by means of the "Come hither" formula.
Regarding the methods for receiving ordination through the *abhisamācārikā* (higher training), the Saṃgha, or the Buddha:
when the Buddha was present, there was the method of receiving the precepts by the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) address; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this no longer exists.
Ordination is obtained through the three utterances.
While residing among the great assembly of monks,
prior to the performance of the *karmavācanā*, it is permitted;
however, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, it is not permitted to receive the precepts through question and answer.
If, in the present age of the Final Dharma, there should be a śrāmaṇera named Sudāya,
he is also permitted to receive the precepts and obtain ordination through the Eight Rules of Respect;
however, this does not apply to the single person, Ānanda’s sister, who dwells among the bhikṣuṇīs.
Others obtain the precepts through being sent by another;
this applies only to the nun Upāliṃdā of Vārāṇasī.
If there should be such a bhikṣu in these final times, [he too shall obtain them].
One must not allow even the slightest [transgression] regarding the listening [of the precepts].
As for the five men of the borderlands attaining the precepts:
today, the Buddha-dharma exists in the border regions.

In the beginning, all initial practices were permitted; those who had previously married and were twelve years of age were placed at the head of the assembly of nuns, and their reception of the precepts was common to both monks and nuns.
Now, if there are those who have attained the state of an Arhat, [the same applies].
This is also what is termed "precept" (*śīla*).

Only the single method of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is a teaching that universally applies to both ordinary persons and sages, reaching both monks and nuns, and encompassing both the present and the future; one must know its formal procedures.
Because it is established through the non-establishment [of its opposite], this is explained in detail according to the various schools. Question:
How many conditions must the *karmavācanā* for receiving full ordination possess in order to be designated as "in accordance with the Dharma"? Answer:
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, six conditions must be fulfilled for the procedure to be established as lawful. What are these six?
First, the person receiving the precepts must be at least twenty-three years of age and possess both robes and a bowl.
Second, the person receiving the precepts must be free from the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*).
Third, it is necessary that the fruit be realized and accomplished.
Fourth, all the monks within the boundary (*sīmā*) must assemble.
Fifth, there is no separate assembly.
Sixth, the *karmavācanā* recites the text exactly as it stands, without addition or omission.
Seventh, ten monks are present, being complete in number, in accordance with the Dharma, and pure.
When these six conditions are complete, one is said to have received the precepts in accordance with the Dharma.
If even one of these six is lacking, the reception of the precepts is not accomplished. Question:
How is it that one’s age is considered to have reached twenty? Answer:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One must be twenty years of age;
[this refers to] having completed twenty rains."
If one has reached twenty years of age,
but is not yet twenty at the time of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one does not obtain the precepts;
however, provided that the *varṣā* is completed, one may receive the precepts.
If one is born in winter and receives the precepts after the summer retreat has concluded,
this is called being less than twenty years old.
If one is born in spring and receives the precepts after the [spring] retreat has concluded, [it is likewise].
This is called being twenty years of age.
If one is born at the conclusion of the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (early rains) retreat, one receives the precepts upon the conclusion of that preceding *anvārambhaṇa* retreat.
If one is born during the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* (late rains) retreat, one receives the precepts upon the conclusion of that subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* retreat.
This is called being twenty years old.
According to the system of the *Caturvargika*, twelve months constitute one year;
for those who are twenty years old, the month of their birth is taken as the basis for calculation.
All are said to receive the full ordination upon reaching twenty years of age.
According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, one receives the full ordination directly upon completing twenty rains-retreats;
for example, one born in the twelfth month reaches twenty years of age by passing through eighteen rains-retreats.
Therefore, it is called "incomplete.
In such cases, one must wait until after twenty years of *varṣa* have been fulfilled before being permitted to receive the precepts.
Furthermore, the matter of receiving the precepts is of great gravity.
This is the very foundation of going forth.
If the original rite is not accomplished, one is not a bhikṣu;
it would be no different from relying on a mere formal declaration (śuklavidhi).
To accept the offerings of faith and prostrations from others is in every case termed theft;
one incurs immeasurable transgression.
If a person knows for certain that one who has received the precepts is younger than themselves,
even if they have passed a hundred years [of age], they are still called a śrāmaṇera;
such a person should not receive the prostrations of a great bhikṣu, nor should they accept offerings from the faithful.
Regarding the Receiving of Ordination Again: Question.
Since receiving this [initial] ordination, one has already fully undergone the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* rituals.
For what reason may one receive the ordination again? Answer.
This constitutes the formal act (*karman*) for receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
It is intended to authorize the *poṣadha* ceremony;
it is not because one listens with a thieving mind. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one may receive the precepts again. Answer.
Jizang said:
"If a person does not know their own age, they should ask their parents or relatives;
if they still do not know, they should consult the birth register."
If there is no such [record], one should observe his facial features and whether his hands and feet are well-formed.
If they do not correspond [to the description], and one does not know [the answer], one should ask:
"Which king? In what year? Was the land abundant or impoverished? Was there drought or flooding? and so forth.
It is not meant that all such things are uniquely difficult to know.
If one investigates each of these one by one and truly does not know them, even after twenty years have passed.
Even if one’s hands and feet are fully formed, one still does not obtain the precepts. Question:
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that if one has not reached twenty years of age...
Regarding the counting of the months of conception, the months of moisture, and so forth:
what follows this? Answer:
There are those who, at the time they first receive the precepts...
The meaning is that when he had completed twenty years of age and finished receiving the precepts, he realized they were actually not yet full;
harboring doubts, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to count the months of gestation and the months of conception.
If one counts all fourteen-day periods, this constitutes the recitation of the precepts."
If one has reached the full number of years, there is no offense;
this is what the Great Sage opened up so that one may obtain the precepts.
According to the laws of this country, [the soil] is moistened again every five years. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
King Bimbisāra undergoes a moistening once every six years;
the Pañcavargīyas undergo a moistening once every five years.

It is not known which of these is definitive. [Question: Why must the second point regarding the absence of obstacles in one’s physical person be asked? [Answer: [The answer continues: Because... (as per the source text).
The thirteen difficult questions are categorized into three groups that pull one away, creating a separation from the Noble Path.
Because these act as obstacles to the arising of the precepts, they are called "difficulties.
Therefore, it is necessary to ask them. Furthermore, [the following] question is asked:
What are the names and meanings of the thirteen difficulties? Answer:
First is the difficulty of the offense of a single defeat (pārājika).
This person has previously received the full precepts (mahā-śīla).
Having committed a *pārājika* offense, he was expelled from the Saṃgha;
later, having returned of his own accord, he was ordained again,
though he remained excluded from the community.
The first is called the obstacle of the boundary, which prevents the arising of the precepts;
it is termed a "difficulty.
The second is the obstacle of a nun who has defiled her pure conduct.
One who has not committed sexual misconduct since going forth from home is said to possess pure conduct; however,
if one committed such an offense while still a layperson, [the status is different].
For this reason, such a person is called "difficult.
Third is the difficulty of receiving the precepts with a thievish mind:
such a person shaves their own hair without a teacher.
Wearing the kashaya without having received the precepts,
yet participating in the uposatha and other formal acts (karmavācanā) with others, one secretly steals the Buddha-dharma; therefore,
this is called the "thieving mind."

If those belonging to the three lower assemblies listen to the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts and falsely claim to participate in the affairs of the Saṅgha, they also commit an offense.
This is the fourth difficulty regarding the breaking of internal and external paths.
This person was originally a non-Buddhist who came to renounce the world;
after receiving the precepts, he did not relinquish them,
yet returned to join the non-Buddhists.
If one’s mind of wrong views is heavy,
one naturally loses the precepts;
if such a person wishes again to seek ordination and receive the precepts within the Buddha-dharma, this is called "difficult."
Fifth is the difficulty regarding eunuchs.
Such persons have many afflictions and lack the observance of the precepts.
Because the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are heavy and one does not generate the Great Precepts (*mahā-śīla*),
it is called a "difficulty.
Sixth is the difficulty of killing one's father.
Seventh is the hardship of killing one's mother.
Whether it be a layperson killing their father or killing their mother,
such an act violates the depth of gratitude and constitutes a profound obstacle.
The non-arising of the precepts:
the eighth obstacle is killing an Arhat;
while he was a layman, he killed a bhikṣu.
At the time of death, his complexion remained unchanged.
Ninth, he caused a schism in the Sangha by falsely preaching heterodox teachings.
Or they may disturb the minds of the multitude by performing separate religious rites within the same boundary,
thereby severing and destroying the Buddha-dharma.
To act intentionally after having known [the consequences] is therefore called "difficult. This is the tenth:
the difficulty of shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
This person, employing skillful means, intended to kill the Buddha,
yet he was unable to sever his life-force and only succeeded in injuring the holy body.
Violating the principles of reason is profound;
one incurs the grave crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
In this present age of the final dharma, people burn and destroy monasteries, images, and relics.
If one sees such auspicious signs, one also incurs the grave offense of opposition and cannot receive the precepts; therefore,
this is called a "difficulty."
Eleventh is the obstacle of non-humans (*amanuṣya*).
If a ghost (*preta*) or a deva transforms themselves into human form with the desire to receive the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*),
this is called the obstacle of non-humans.
Twelfth is the difficulty of being among animals.
Whether they be dragons or foxes who have transformed themselves into human form,
they may not receive the precepts.
Thirteen: The difficulty regarding those with two sexual organs.
Such a person possesses both male and female organs;
they have no place of assignment within either of the two assemblies, the monks or the nuns.
Therefore, they are called "difficult.
Among these thirteen types of persons, the first four and those with the obstacle of karmic hindrance from the five heinous crimes are subsumed under karmic obstacles;
the one who is a eunuch is subsumed under the obstacle of afflictions.
The latter three are subsumed under the "obstacles that report.
Bound by these three obstacles within a single lifetime, they cannot be altered.
Those who have not yet left the household life must not be ordained; those who have already left the household life should be expelled.
A detailed explanation is as set forth in the treatise. Question:
Are the thirteen difficulties not considered to constitute the precepts? Answer: No.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"After [the prohibition] was established, one cannot receive the precepts. It further asks:
"Was it not originally for the purpose of preventing difficulties?"
"Now, if it truly does not exist, why is there a need to ask? Answer:
"Although it is difficult to do so, one must ask.
If it truly exists, one will not obtain the precepts whether one asks or does not ask."
If there are truly no obstacles or questions, one obtains the precepts;

if there are questions, one does not obtain them. Third, the clarification of the establishment of the boundary (sīmā-bandha), including the method for re-establishing it when it has not been successfully formed, shall be explained later. Fourth, the entire Saṃgha within the boundary must assemble.
Those who do not come must grant their consent so that the community of monks remains in harmony and there is no separate faction. Regarding the fifth *karmavācanā*, as for reciting the text:
if one performs a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
Furthermore, if there are five, three, two, or one white [robes], none of these constitute a valid quorum. Regarding the sixth requirement for the full number of the Saṃgha:
it must consist of ten pure, fully ordained bhikṣus.
If there are more than ten people, it is called a "community" (*saṃgha*);
if the number is full or less, it is not established. Question:
Can a person who has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) or one of the thirteen types of persons with impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) serve as an upādhyāya?
Question: Is the precept obtained? Answer:
The *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states:
"This person does not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha; the precept is not obtained."
As for the remaining witnesses who have committed grave offenses, it is sufficient that there be many witnesses so that one obtains the precepts;
if there are few, one does not obtain them. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
At that time, there was one who had received the precepts from an upādhyāya who did not maintain the precepts.
Later, he gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha asked him:
"Do you know whether your preceptor maintains the precepts?
He replied,
"I do not know."
The Buddha said,
"Yes; this is called receiving the full precepts."
Furthermore, there were those who received the precepts from an upādhyāya who did not maintain the precepts.
The Buddha asked them,
"Do you know whether your upādhyāya maintains the precepts or not?"
He replied,
"I know.
You know that you should not receive full ordination from such a person."
He replied,
"I do not know.
The Buddha said:
This is called receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, later there was a householder who questioned the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Do you know that your preceptor has broken the precepts?
He replied,
"I know."
"Do you know that one should not receive the precepts from a person who has broken the precepts?
He replied,
"I know."
The Buddha said,
"Do you know that one cannot receive the precepts from a person who has broken the precepts?
He replied:
"I do not know.
The Buddha said, "He is considered to have received full ordination. As for the fourth person, who knows all three points:
This is not called receiving the full ordination. Question:
Can one receive the precepts without a preceptor?
The Buddha said:
It is not permitted.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: Upāli asked.
"Can one receive full ordination without a preceptor?
The Buddha said,
"One may be said to have received full ordination."
The *karmavācanā* officiant and the assembly of monks may be guilty of offenses.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there was an upādhyāya who, being nine years old, conferred full ordination upon others."
"I do not know whether the ordination has been successfully accomplished.
The Buddha said,
"The ordination is successfully accomplished."
The Sangha has committed an offense. Question:
Is it permissible to receive the precepts if one lacks a robe and bowl?
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who lacks a robe and bowl may not receive the precepts. He asked again, "May one who borrows a robe and bowl receive the precepts?
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
One who borrows robes and a bowl should be instructed by the owner of the robes to relinquish them [as a formal gift] before they may receive the precepts.
The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Can one receive the precepts without possessing a robe and bowl?
He replied,
"One can."
If that is so, what need is there for robes and alms bowls?
He replied:
"Firstly, it is for the sake of proper deportment."
Second, it is for the sake of generating merit for those who have passed away;
second, it is to distinguish it from other [requisites].
Thus, one must possess both robe and bowl.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
"If one counts the preceptor as the tenth person in the quorum,
it is not called the conferral of full ordination."
Furthermore, one does not state one's own name,
nor does one state the name of one's preceptor,
nor does one request the precepts.
None of these are said to have received full ordination.
One who acts as an upādhyāya for others must possess ten virtues;
the first is observance of the precepts.
Second, being well-versed in the Abhidharma;
third, being well-versed in the Vinaya;
fourth, training in the precepts.
Fifth, training in meditative concentration;
sixth, training in wisdom;
seventh, training in purifying one's own offenses and causing others to purify their offenses.
Eighth, he is able to tend to the sick himself.
Ninth, if a disciple faces difficulties regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
he is able to escort them himself or send someone to escort them so they may escape those difficulties.
When ten years have been completed and ten years of seniority attained, one may leave the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and rely upon an *ācārya*; such an *ācārya* should possess ten qualities:
first, he must fully maintain the two hundred and fifty precepts;
second, he must be widely learned.
Third, he is able to instruct his disciples in the Abhidharma;
fourth, he is able to instruct his disciples in the Vinaya;
fifth, he is able to instruct his disciples to abandon evil and cultivate right view.
Sixth, knowing the *prātimokṣa* precepts;
seventh, knowing how to recite the *prātimokṣa* precepts;
eighth, knowing how to perform the *poṣadha*.
Ninth, knowing how to perform the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā*.
Tenth, having completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), one may emerge from the *Caturvarga* [Vinaya].

The same applies to the ten virtues of the *upādhyāya* during the period of increasing by ten years. Regarding the two types of *karmavācanā* for ritual decorum (*īryāpatha*), the *ācārya* should possess five virtues.
First, knowing the superior code of conduct is the purification of the precepts of body and speech;
it is also called the *saṃvara-śīla*. Second, knowing the superior purity of practice is the purification of the precepts of mind;
it is also called the *samādhi-sahagata-śīla*. Third, knowing the superior *prātimokṣa* precepts is the purification of the precepts of wisdom.
It is also called the "precept concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*).

Because supramundane dharmas transcend mundane dharmas, they are said to be "superior. The phrase "The four knowledges [arise] from one's own *karma*" indicates that this single sentence is perfected in its phrasing as a wholesome communal legal act (*saṃghakarma*).
The words clarify that one who has attained proficiency must have five full years of ordination—that is, five years of training in the precepts.

When one's own practice is perfected, they are capable of acting as a teacher for others. One who presides over the *dāna* ceremony and witnesses the recipient should be endowed with these five virtues.
First, being well-versed in matters that involve obstacles;
second, being well-versed in matters that are free from obstacles;
third, being well-versed in the formal procedure of making a motion (*jñapti*).
Fourth, being skilled in performing *karmavācanā* (formal acts).
Fifth, having pure conduct regarding the precepts.

One who possesses these five virtues is capable of presiding over the formal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) and attesting to the dignity of the assembly. There are five conditions under which one must not remain without a formal reliance (*niśraya*).
First, one cannot diligently cultivate the precepts of dignified conduct; second, one cannot increase pure conduct;
third, one cannot increase the *prātimokṣa* precepts;
fourth, if one possesses evil views, one cannot abandon them and abide in right view.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* state:
"A bhikṣu who has completed five years and has accomplished five qualities is permitted to dwell without receiving formal reliance (*niśraya*)."
First, knowing what constitutes an offense;
second, knowing what does not constitute an offense;
third, knowing what is light.
Fourth, knowing the gravity [of the precepts].
Fifth, reciting the Prātimokṣa for its benefits.
If these five qualities are lacking:
Even if one has lived for many years or until the end of one’s life depending on another for residence, it is asked:
"May a great bhikṣu live in dependence upon a junior bhikṣu? The answer is: "He may."
Except for the act of prostration, all other matters follow the rules for disciples.

There are five conditions under which one loses reliance upon a preceptor: first, the death of the teacher; second, his passing away; third, his departure; fourth, his renunciation of the preceptor; and fifth, the student’s own renunciation of the preceptor.
If the preceptor stays overnight at a distance, or if the disciple resolves to go outside the boundary, or if the three [conditions] for leaving the path are met;

if the preceptor relinquishes the precepts, or if the four conditions for not granting dependence arise, or if the teacher abandons instruction; or if one returns to dwell under the direct supervision of the *upādhyāya*.
If the upādhyāya has already accepted [the disciple],
the ācārya should not be asked to provide instruction and admonition.
This is the rule for dependence (*niśraya*) established in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Even to the point where one was unable to seek water for washing or rinsing;
because [the disciple] first sought formal reliance [upasthāpanā] and subsequently failed to recognize the signs of transgression,
the Buddha granted permission [to provide such assistance].
Even regarding the allowance for staying overnight together, if it involves remaining without formal dependence (*niśraya*), this is not permitted.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Upāli had two śrāmaṇeras who wished to receive the precepts through the simultaneous performance of the *karmavācanā*.
He informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Those who share the same preceptor (upādhyāya) are permitted.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four kinds of teachers.

1. If there is neither Dharma nor food, one may depart without needing to inquire; 2. If there is no Dharma but there is food and clothing, one must inquire before departing; 3. If there is no food or clothing but there is Dharma, one should remain despite the hardship; 4. If there is Dharma and there is food and clothing, this is a pleasant dwelling. Regarding the first two types of teachers:
If one cannot perform the formal confession and apology before departing,
there are five faults in being unable to leave the teacher for as long as one lives, provided that the latter two types of teachers possess the Dharma.
After the disciple has finished the confession and apology, they should depart and say to the preceptor one of the following two things:
"I have acted according to the Dharma, but the preceptor did not know," or "I have not acted according to the Dharma, but the preceptor did not know."
Third, when I have committed an offense, I abandon it and fail to instruct or reprove others.
Fourth, even if I commit an offense, I do not recognize it as such.
Fifth, once an offense has been committed, I repent of it.
Furthermore, this does not equal the benefit of having already left the household life and being trained to completion.
For this reason, one requests [instruction] while remaining outside [the monastic community].
Although there are many kinds of superior dharmas to be consulted and studied, as well as the precepts to be received according to one's faculties, [these are the primary concerns].
In sum, the essential point is that it consists of both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
Initially, one forms the intention to receive the precepts before a teacher;
through the movement of body and speech, this dharma is brought into being.
This is called "the precept of action.
Once the attainment of the precept has been ruined,
it no longer functions within the mind and is no longer cultivated.
Therefore, it is called the unconditioned precept (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*).
This supramundane dharma is received through the formation of a volitional mind,
and one may likewise abandon it through the formation of a volitional mind.
One would then lose one's wholesome karma;
otherwise, it must necessarily bring about its retribution,
which is not the case with the dharmas of the precepts.
There is the sense of relinquishment.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there were those who did not confer the śrāmaṇera precepts but instead conferred full ordination directly."
"I do not know whether it is accomplished or not.
The Buddha said,
"It is fully accomplished."
Regarding the transgressions of the Saṃgha,
the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"At that time, there were those who received the precepts from a teacher who had broken the precepts."
He raised a doubt with the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Did you first ascertain whether your preceptor had received the precepts from his own teacher?"
He replied,
"I do not know.
The Buddha said:
Receiving the Name of Precepts. Question:
May a *bhikṣu* confer the six rules and the ten precepts upon a *bhikṣuṇī*?
Answer: [He may.]
The great monks may perform only three types of *karmavācanā* for a *bhikṣuṇī*: first, the formal act of ordination (*upasaṃpadā*);
second, the *mānatva* penance.
Third is the expiation of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).
Regarding all other ritual matters (*dharmakarma*), there are no textual records in the various Vinayas;
even if one were to perform them, the *karmavācanā* would not be validly accomplished.
Monks and Nuns Committing Offenses. Question:
For what reason do Great Nīs (Mahābhikṣuṇīs) take Bhikṣus as their teachers, while Śikṣamāṇās and Śrāmaṇerīs do not? Answer:
Women do not possess independent resolve;
therefore, the Sages established the rule that one receiving the full ordination must take a member of the Great Sangha as preceptor.
Or there may be śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs who have recently left the household life,
being young in age and weak in resolve;
they rely solely upon a mahābhikṣuṇī as their preceptor.
Question: When receiving the six rules (ṣaḍ-dharmāḥ) as part of training in the precepts, is it necessary to invite a *upādhyāya*? Answer: No.
It is not necessary. Why is this so?
Because a śikṣamāṇā merely adds six out of the eight [precepts] to the ten precepts for further study.
Since this is not yet a case of changing one's position, there is no need to request [permission].
Furthermore, all four divisions of the Vinaya state that it refers to a place where one can see with the eyes but cannot hear with the ears.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) face-to-face [with another], the reception of the six dharmas is not accomplished, and one incurs an offense.
Question: Some say that...
"Is it according to the Dharma for a great bhikṣuṇī to pay homage to a śrāmaṇera? [The Buddha] replied:
"This person does not understand the characteristics of the Vinaya."
This is a false assertion.
Why? Because in the *Vihāravastu* (Chapter on Dwellings) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it says:
The Buddha himself established the rules of reverence for the bhikṣus:
even a junior śrāmaṇera should pay homage to a senior śrāmaṇerī,
let alone a bhikṣuṇī who would not pay homage.
Who are those who should not be saluted? Those with the thirteen grounds for censure,
those who have been formally accused, those who have been expelled, and those who speak what is contrary to the Dharma— such persons as these should not be saluted.
In such a case, both parties incur an offense. Next, the method for relinquishing the precepts is explained.
Since the precepts are a pure dharma that should be requested, ascended, and manifested, the fivefold assembly of monks and nuns must uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
It is better to die than to commit an offense.
If one should intentionally commit an offense, it would be no different from never having left the household life at all. Why is this?
They destroy the Dharma of the Path themselves,
bring disgrace upon their teachers and the Sangha,
and defile and disorder the Triple Gem.
To deceive those who contemplate the four truths is a grave offense;
it does not merely render the offerings of the faithful fruitless,
but results in even greater transgression.
If a person’s mind is oppressed by afflictions,
their inclination toward the Path is weak,
and they are unable to restrain themselves from committing evil when they so desire; [they should practice this].
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to renounce the precepts and return home;
you must not rely upon or depend on the Buddha-dharma."
This constitutes a violation of the pure prohibitions.
If one wishes to relinquish the precepts,
one should do so before a single bhikṣu.
Therefore, kneeling with palms joined,
one speaks these words:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind."
I, the bhikṣu [Name],
now relinquish the great [precepts] and return to being a layperson.
I pray that the Virtuous One will grant me his protection.
"I am a white-robed layperson.
Thus one says three times.
If one wishes to retain the five precepts:
One should say:
"I return to being a lay follower (upāsaka).
If you wish to retain the ten precepts," [one should say].
I declare that I have returned to being a śrāmaṇera;
may the Venerable One bear this in mind.
"I am a śrāmaṇera.
Originally, I received the precepts from the Saṃgha;
now I should likewise return them to the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma."
The Saṃgha shall then bear witness to this.

This [act] cannot be relinquished in the presence of others; if it is a bhikṣuṇī, she must return to the community of nuns to relinquish it. If, after having relinquished the precepts, one again finds joy in the Buddha-dharma and wishes to go forth, [the procedure is as follows].
They are permitted to return to the life of a layperson,
but nuns are not permitted to do so. Why is this?
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*,
it is recorded that when a layperson saw a bhikṣuṇī who had returned to secular life, he reviled her, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī formerly held my Dharma in high esteem."
In the past, he was respected by me;
now, in turn, he respects me.
There is no fixed certainty in this.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If a bhikṣuṇī returns the precepts even once."
They shall no longer be permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
Part Three: The Method for Establishing Boundaries as Clarified in the Vinayas and Treatises of the Four Schools. Regarding boundaries, there are two kinds.
First, the constructed boundary;
second, the natural boundary.
Regarding the constructed boundary:
The boundary is established through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* performed by the Saṃgha;
therefore, it is called a "formally established boundary" (*kṛta-sīmā*).
As for the "natural boundary" (*prakṛti-sīmā*):
It exists spontaneously without depending on the formation of a conscious mind;
therefore, it is called the "natural realm" (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding the four divisions of the Vinaya texts, they differ in their mutual arrangements.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
Regarding the natural boundary of a village:
it extends five hundred *dhanus* from the village;
one *dhanu* is the length of four cubits (*hasta*) of an average person. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Outside the village, for the distance of one arrow-shot,
including the areas where those who feel shame (the laity) perform their bodily functions,
is called the "natural boundary" (*prakṛtisīmā*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The area outside the village where cattle and sheep roam freely is called the "natural boundary of the settlement" (*grāma-sīmā*).
It is also said:
Regarding the seven trees:
the dharma of boundary-establishment (sīmā-bandha) cannot be performed [there],
because a boundary does not yet exist.
One resident bhikṣu shall chant the boundaries three times; then,
when performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to establish the boundary,
it shall extend as far as the natural limits of the area.
The boundary is established only when the entire Saṃgha has assembled;
if they do not assemble, the establishment of the boundary is not accomplished.
If the boundary is not established, [the ritual is invalid].
If one performs any ritual acts of the Dharma, such as receiving the precepts, within this area, they will all be invalid.
If the boundary for not losing one's robes (asatthakāra-sīmā) has not yet been established,
then from outside the great boundary (mahāsīmā), it extends as far as a stone thrown by an average person can reach.
Regarding the natural boundary for the non-forfeiture of robes:
if the observance of the non-forfeiture of robes has been formally established, there is no natural boundary for the non-forfeiture of robes. Question: [What is the case] when...?
Regarding the three divisions of the *vidyā*:
the natural realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not fixed.
If the monks within the natural realm do not assemble, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) will not be accomplished.
Various masters have stated that [the self] is established, while others have stated that it is not established.
Now, which school’s position shall be taken as definitive? Answer:
Regarding the natural realm of the three vidyās:
it is not a naturally established boundary,
but rather the natural realm of solitary dwelling.
This is explained in order to clarify the distinct reasons for defining the two boundaries of open space and inhabited villages. Question:
What constitutes the natural boundary (*dharmatā-sīmā*)? Answer: [As follows].
Other vinayas do not provide further explicit clarification.
Now, I shall clarify the natural boundaries for the formal demarcation of the *sīmā* according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who asked the Buddha for the method of planting mango trees.
The Buddha then answered him.
At that time, Upāli, knowing the proper occasion, asked the Buddha, saying:
"I have already heard the measurement of the āmra fruit;
I now ask again for further instruction."
If there is a location— such as a city, town, or village— where the boundaries cannot be determined,
and one wishes to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā), to what extent must it be defined so that the ritual is considered properly performed?
This allows members of different assemblies to see one another and thereby accomplish the *karmavācanā* without committing the offense of performing it separately from the assembly.
The Buddha told Upāli:
The measurement of a bow is five cubits;
plant mango trees at intervals of seven bows from one another.
This is the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) to be performed.
This is called a *karmavācanā* performed properly.
Although the members of the assembly may see one another differently, there is no separate meal for a distinct group;
[the space] is one cubit (one *hasta*) and eight inches, or five cubits long, which is nine feet.
Between each tree there is ten paces and a half.
Calculating for seven trees, there are seventy-three paces and a half. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"In the *Upāli-paripṛcchā*, it is asked:"
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu constructs a monastery in a village where no monastery previously existed,
and has not yet performed the formal delimitation of the boundary (sīmābandha)."
"To what extent is it called a boundary?
The Buddha said,
"It is the extent of the common thoroughfare belonging to this village boundary."
He asked again:
"If a bhikṣu first establishes a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma) in a forest hermitage (araṇya) where there is no village,
before the boundary has been demarcated..."
Regarding this, to what extent is it called a "boundary"?
The Buddha said:
"One krośa on each side."
In this matter, the bhikṣus should assemble in their entirety to perform the *karmavācanā*.
If they perform it as a separate assembly, all the bhikṣus incur an offense. One *krośa* is equivalent to five *li*.
"If a bhikṣu relinquishes the great boundary (mahā-sīmā),
does he also relinquish the zone where robes may not be left behind (a-cīvara-apahāra-sīmā)?
The Buddha said, "He also relinquishes it."
He asked again:
"If one relinquishes the *acīvara-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe),
is the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary) also relinquished?"
The Buddha said, "It is not relinquished. He asked,
"If one does not relinquish a previous boundary, may another— whether large or small— be established?"
The Buddha said it is not permitted. The four directions clearly demarcate ten kinds of boundaries, each having its own natural sphere of influence (*sīmā*).
Regarding the boundary of a monastery (*saṃghārāma-sīmā*), there are four types.
First, there is the surrounding wall;
second, the inner palisade;
third, the outer palisade—these three are not the same.
The surrounding houses and the two tree boundaries:
that is to say, the area covered by the shade of trees is called the tree boundary.
Third is the field boundary;
this refers to the area within which the five grains are cultivated.
Fourth is the cart boundary.
This refers to the place where a vehicle turns back.
Fifth is the boat boundary;
this refers to the place where a boat turns back.
The boundary of the six villages is of four kinds,
as explained in the case of the monastery (ārāma).
Seventh is the boundary of the dwelling (śayanāsana-sīmā), within which laypeople and their wives and children reside.
Eighth is the boundary of the storehouse (koṣṭhaka-sīmā).
Among these, the places where things are accumulated are the nine hall-elements (*koṣṭhā-dhātu*) and the ten storehouse-elements (*kośa-dhātu*).
Regarding the place where the five grains are stored, these ten types of boundaries each extend from their respective borders as far as a stone can be thrown five times;
this is called the "natural boundary for robes. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If one is traveling on water,
the boundary established by the range of water sprinkled by a strong person among the assembly may extend as far as three yojanas;
this is the maximum distance for the ritual of establishing a boundary.
Beyond this, it is not permitted. The *Sāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Shanjian lun) states that for the smallest boundary site (*sīmā*), twenty-one guests may be accommodated.

Furthermore, the *Sāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* clarifies that among the eight types of objects used to mark the boundaries, there are those where the boundary is validly established and those where it is not.
First is the characteristic of the mountain boundary (*parvata-sīmā-lakṣaṇa*).
The large is like Mount Sumeru;
the small extends downward to the size of a bird.
Second, the boundary markers for the stone area:
the large ones are like oxen;
the small ones are thirty *tsubo* in size.
One must not use scattered stones as boundary markers;
rather, one should place separate stones [for each].
Third, the boundary marker consisting of three groves of trees.
The large ones are one hundred yojanas in extent;
the small ones extend downward to as little as four trees joined together,
and these are also called forests.
Bamboo and grass may not be used as boundary markers because their substance is empty and insubstantial.
Fourth, tree boundary markers.
The large [trees] are like those of Jambudvīpa;
the small are as low as eight inches and as thick as a needle, and they may serve to establish a boundary.
If there are no naturally grown trees, planting trees will also suffice.
A withered tree may not be used as a boundary marker (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the boundary markers for the five paths:
one may establish a marker for a carriage path, a cattle path, or even a trail that passes through three or four villages.
If one enters a field, a path leading toward a well, a path leading toward a river, or a cul-de-sac, these cannot serve as boundary markers (*sīmā-nimitta*).
Sixth, ant-hills (*valmīka*) may serve as boundary markers;
the large ones are like mountains.
The smallest measures eight inches at most;
it is sufficient to establish the boundary markers.
There are seven types of river boundary markers.
If a good king governs and transforms the realm,
rain falls twice every five days;
such river water cannot serve as a boundary marker.
If it does not rain for four months,
the river water flows constantly without interruption;
when the depth of the water reaches two feet, it may be used as a boundary marker.
Regarding the eight characteristics of the water-element boundary:
if it is the water of a natural pond, it may serve as a boundary marker;
however, water from a conduit entering a field or water contained in a vessel cannot serve as a boundary marker.
These are called the eight kinds.
After the boundary has been demarcated by means of these eight kinds of boundary marks,
although the boundary marks may perish, the boundary itself is not lost.
If a person digs down to the water's edge, it is likewise not lost. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there was a bhikṣu who did not announce the boundaries."
One should establish the boundary by means of the four directions,
or by using sentient beings, smoke, fire, and so forth as the boundary markers.
The Buddha said:
The boundary is not established, nor is the demarcation of the boundary established;
one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

A bhikṣuṇī may establish a boundary of only one krośa, whereas the saṃgha boundary is ten krośas. Question: For what reason, when establishing the robe boundary (cīvara-sīmā), is it specifically stated that the village and its precincts are excluded? Answer: [The answer follows: Because the robe boundary is established for the purpose of protecting the robes from being lost or stolen; since the village is a place where robes are frequently left behind or where theft occurs, it is therefore excluded.

Furthermore, the robe boundary is intended to facilitate the practice of the *pārivāsika* (probation) and *mānāpya* (rehabilitation) penances, and since these practices require the monks to remain within the boundary together, the village—which is a place of distraction—is excluded so as not to hinder their observance of the rules. Thus, the exclusion of the village and its precincts is established solely for the sake of maintaining the integrity of the robe boundary.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
A village is characterized by distraction and lack of fixed boundaries,
whereas the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is fixed.
Therefore, it must be removed.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of removing slander,
and for the sake of removing strife and contention.
Because it protects the holy life (brahmacarya), it is therefore excluded.
Question: In a village, there must be exclusion; in a non-village, why is there exclusion? Answer: [It is because...]
This is the nature of the *karmavācanā* procedure.
If there were no exemptions for all [cases], why would this be so?
If, at the time of the formal boundary-establishment, there was no village and the boundary has been completed when a village subsequently enters it,
there is no need for a further establishment,
as the previous one remains valid.
If a village originally existed and was later moved elsewhere,
this very empty space is called the "boundary not separated from the robe.
If a village was originally small and later became large...
Wherever there are villages or locations, these are all not robe-boundaries (cīvara-sīmā).
If the area was previously large and subsequently becomes small,
then wherever there is empty space, it is entirely a robe-boundary.
It is further said:
"Just as when a king enters the precincts of a monastery,
he pitches a tent and stays nearby to the left or right, where food is prepared."
All places of walking, whether large or small, are not robe-boundaries (*cīvara-sīmā*). Question:
If a bhikṣuṇī does not further establish a boundary within the boundary of the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*), may she perform ritual acts (*dharmakarma*) there? Answer: Yes.
The formal ritual procedures cannot be accomplished because the boundaries of the monks and nuns are distinct and do not encompass one another.
One should further establish [the rules]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), if there are dangers such as kings, bandits, threats to life, or obstacles to the holy life;
or if there is much water containing insects that cannot be strained out and purified."
One may establish boundaries at will for three *śīti*s (thirty days) in each of the four directions.

If a difficulty should suddenly arise and one is unable to perform the *karmavācanā* ritual before departing, there is no offense in leaving the boundaries of all directions. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
When monks perform the formal ritual for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha-karman*),
if the entire Saṃgha transforms their gender and becomes women,
it is called a "monk's boundary."
This is called the boundary of the bhikṣuṇīs.
When a boundary is demarcated, there may be parts that change and parts that do not;
what is the name of such a boundary?
The Buddha said:
"When other monks have transferred their status as the *karmakāraka* (the one who performs the formal act) while this person has not,
it is called the 'monk's boundary' (*bhikṣusīma*)."
If the person performing the *karmavācanā* changes into a woman,
it is called the boundary of the bhikṣuṇīs.
The same applies to whether the boundary established by bhikṣuṇīs is maintained or not.

4. The Karmavācanā Methods as Clarified in the Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries. Section Four: Regarding the texts of the various Vinayas, they simply state that there are one hundred and one *karmas*.

This refers to the *jñapti* (single motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion followed by three proclamations) which do not conclude with the formal announcement of the matter.
Now, according to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, their specific numbers are set forth:
there are twenty-four types of *jñapti*.
There are thirty [procedures] involving one motion and three proclamations;
these constitute one hundred and one.
There are twenty-four [procedures] consisting of a single motion.
That is to say: the announcement by the *ācārya* regarding deportment;
the announcement following the *karmavācanā* inquiry concerning obstructive dharmas;
and the announcement at the time of the *poṣadha*.
The announcement that the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense;
the announcement when the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense at the time of the Poṣadha;
and the announcement when one wishes to perform the Pravāraṇā.
The announcement regarding a monk committing an offense during the *pravāraṇā*;
the announcement regarding all monks having doubts concerning an offense during the *pravāraṇā*;
the announcement regarding committing an offense within the midst of all monks during the *pravāraṇā*.
The announcement regarding the determination of the offense during a formal reconciliation;
the announcement at the time of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*);
and the announcement regarding the acceptance of the robe of a deceased bhikṣu alone.
The announcement regarding the distribution of the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu;
the announcement regarding the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe;
and the announcement regarding the confession of a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
The Venerable Dharmabhāṇaka Bhikṣu’s announcement regarding the distribution of robes;
the announcement regarding public censure;
the announcement regarding causing distress or distressing others.
The announcement regarding a householder; the announcement regarding one who has abandoned the status of a householder;
the announcement regarding the overturning of the alms bowl.
The *āśraya-pātra-śukla* (the white procedure concerning the bowl).
These constitute the twenty-four *ekotika-śukla-karman* (single-announcement white procedures).
Regarding the forty-seven [procedures] that are two-fold white:
That is to say: the formal motion for the *poṣadha* performed in the presence [of the assembly];
the formal motion for the ritual of binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*);
and the formal motion for binding the robe boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
The formal motion with announcement for delimiting a small boundary;
the formal motion with announcement regarding those who are insane or deluded;
the formal motion with announcement for appointing a person to preside over the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The formal motion with announcement for the distribution of bedding;
the formal motion with announcement for the demarcation of a pure area;
and the formal motion with announcement for the *kaṭhina* robe.
The formal motion with announcement for receiving the *guṇavastuka-cīvara*;
the formal motion with announcement for keeping the *guṇavastuka-cīvara*;
and the formal motion with announcement for repentance.
A brief explanation of the twelve types of persons who make a formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Regarding the twenty-two persons who make a formal announcement,
the following is annotated below.
That is to say: appointing persons to guard the goods;
appointing the *karmadāna* (steward) to employ people to prepare food and drink according to the Dharma;
and appointing persons to prepare pure fruits and vegetables.
The person who sweeps and cleans,
the person who spreads the bedding for the Sangha,
and the person who distributes the gruel.
The distributor of rice,
the distributor of the two robes, the assigner of duties for novices and gardeners, the *taḷāka* (pool) declaration by *jñapti-dvitīya*,
and the *vita* declaration by *jñapti-dvitīya*.
The white-two motion for settling disputes;
the white-two motion for the distribution of voting tickets (*śalākā*);
the white-two motion for requesting permission to build a hut.
The formal act of two announcements (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the large hall;
the formal act of two announcements by the monk who raises the charge;
the formal act of two announcements by the elder (*sthavira*).
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for relinquishing the alms bowl;
the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for ensuring that laypeople do not lose faith;
and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for appointing a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The white-two-voiced procedure for [a monk] newly arriving;
the white-two-voiced procedure for not performing prostrations;
the white-two-voiced procedure for not conversing.
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for destroying the assembly;
the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for keeping a staff;
the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for keeping a net-bag.
The *jñapti-dvitīya* for obtaining profit after five years;
the *jñapti-dvitīya* for prohibiting the *poṣadha*;
and the *jñapti-dvitīya* for the *śikṣamāṇā* training in the six rules for two years.

The *pūrvakalpa* (former events) concerning the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation): the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* regarding a bhikṣuṇī giving birth in the same room [as a monk],
and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* regarding being in adjoining rooms.
The *jñapti-dvitīya* for the thirty-nine nights;
these are called the forty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya* karmans.
Some teachers say:
All karmas that are to be performed should invariably employ the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion and one proclamation) procedure.
Furthermore, some say that this excludes the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).
All other matters should be handled by the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) procedure.
Regarding the thirty *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations):
this refers to the *jñapti-caturtha* for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the four-month separate residence (*parivāsa*) with non-Buddhists;
the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for relinquishing the three types of boundaries (*sīmā*);
and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the communal *poṣadha* of the various assemblies.
The *jñapti-caturtha* for harsh rebuke;
the *jñapti-caturtha* for dependence;
the *jñapti-caturtha* for expulsion.
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya*) due to not seeing [one's offense];
the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the formal act of suspension due to not removing evil and heterodox views;
and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*).
The formal motion on the day of undertaking the probation is a *jñapti-caturtha*;
the *mānatva* [probation] itself is a *jñapti-caturtha*;
the formal motion on the day of undertaking it is a *jñapti-caturtha*.
The *āpattipratideśana* (confession) *jñapti-caturtha-karman*;
the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection) *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; and the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one not insane) *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
The formal motion with three proclamations for seeking the truth;
the formal motion with three proclamations for schism in the Saṃgha;
and the formal motion with three proclamations for assisting in schism in the Saṃgha.
The *jñapti-caturtha* for wandering;
the *jñapti-caturtha* for acting out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion;
and the *jñapti-caturtha* for harsh speech.
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for one who is evil and heterodox;
the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the expulsion of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*);
and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the suspension of a nun who follows a suspended monk and dwells in defilement.
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the training in the precepts (*śikṣāpada*) is called the thirty *jñapti-caturtha-karmans*. Some say:
All *karmas* should be performed with the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations).
This [present case] consists of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-ekakarma*).
With the exception of the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), all others involve this one motion and one proclamation.
How many are performed by four people? How many are performed by five people?
How many are performed by ten people?
How many are performed by twenty people?
Question: How many people should perform [the formal acts]? Answer:
With the exception of the *pravāraṇā*, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe, and the reception of precepts in border regions, these should be performed by five people.

If there are fewer than these, the four types of *saṃgha* cannot be established. Among them, the *pañcavargīya-saṃgha* consists of five persons for the purpose of conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon two groups.

The *saptadaśavargīya-saṃgha* consists of seventeen persons for the purpose of a monk’s rehabilitation from an offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). The *viṃśativargīya-saṃgha* consists of twenty persons for the purpose of a monk’s rehabilitation from an offense. For the rehabilitation of a nun, it requires twenty persons from each of the two groups.

Excluding the four aforementioned types of *karmavācanā*, all other *karmas* may be performed by a group of four; this is termed a "monastic community of forty. These four types of monastic communities are those who have attained the vehicle of the Dharma.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, speaking of the absolute minimum,
if one exceeds this number it is even better; however,
if they are fewer than this, the rite is not accomplished.
Upāli asked: "If a deaf person is counted among the quorum,
does the formal ritual (karmavācanā) performed constitute a valid ritual?"
Answer: If one hears the motion (*jñapti*), the formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*) is accomplished.
Question:
Question: When performing a *karmavācanā*, if one falls asleep while the *karmavācanā* is being performed, is the *karmavācanā* valid?
Answer:
If one falls asleep after having heard the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the *karmavācanā* is valid.
If, at the time of performing the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*),
the person being banished is asleep but hears the announcement (*jñapti*), the banishment is accomplished.
What constitutes those who do not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha?
The thirteen types of difficult persons:
those who raise objections,
and those who have committed a grave offense.
One who has been expelled;
a layperson; a bhikṣuṇī.
Śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, and śrāmaṇerī.
A person who possesses supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda) remains in the midst of the assembly,
yet they vanish from view;
such a person does not count toward the number of the Saṃgha.
If one fills the required number of the Saṃgha with such persons as these,
the ritual procedure will not be accomplished and one incurs an offense.
Who, then, can suffice to complete the number of the Saṃgha?
If a bhikṣu is pure and acts according to the Dharma, he is said to complete the quorum for the Saṃgha.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* clearly explains five kinds of invalid *karmavācanā* (formal acts) that should not be performed:
first, the *karmavācanā* of an illegal separate assembly; it is called "illegal" because the *karma* is not successfully accomplished.
When the Sangha within a single boundary has not assembled in its entirety, it is called a "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Because it is an illegal concordant assembly (*adharmasāmagrī*) and the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished, it is termed "illegal.
When the Sangha within a single boundary has not assembled in its entirety...
1. It is called a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*); 2. an illegal united assembly where the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished;
3. a legal separate assembly where the *karmavācanā* is accomplished because the entire Saṃgha has assembled;
4. a pseudo-legal separate assembly where the *karmavācanā* is performed upon arrival.
Furthermore, the Saṃgha does not assemble, nor does a group resembling the Dharma in five respects perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*).
Moreover, if a single person utters a rebuke and the *karmavācanā* is not brought to a halt,
one should perform the formal act of reconciliation through such a Dharma-method as follows.
The seventh is the *karmavācanā* for punishing evil persons through disciplinary measures.
First, regarding the *tarjanīya-karman*: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* calls it "subjugation" (*nigraha*).
This person does not internally protect the community.

Because he has caused dissension among the Saṃgha, a *karmavācanā* (formal act) of disciplinary punishment is performed. Second, the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment); in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is called "expulsion.
This person has corrupted and disturbed lay followers.
To cause those who have not yet gained faith to believe,

[the Buddha] spoke this Dharma for the purpose of performing the *karma* of expulsion from the village and the three dependencies for one who has brought disgrace upon the Saṃgha, such as the case of the layman Pāpaka.
Because they do not guard themselves within,

this *karmavācanā* was established as a regulation to cause them to study the Vinaya and receive instruction; in the Mahāsāṃghika school, this is called the "non-speaking *karmavācanā*" (*anālāpa-karman*), which constitutes one of the four prohibitions.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* refer to the *karmavācanā* for not visiting the homes of laypeople as "lowering one's mind" (*mīngxià-yì*);
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls it "arousing joy.
Such a person does not possess external protection or firm faith.
Since this lay follower has already placed faith [in the Dharma], one should cause it to increase;
therefore, perform this *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) to restrain him.
This person shall not be permitted to go himself; instead, another monk of virtuous conduct shall be specially appointed.

Regarding the reconciliation and apology to laypeople for the five cases of not acknowledging an offense during the *karma* of formal accusation (*ukkhittaka*), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Not acknowledging [the offense], one is suspended.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: [Not acknowledging the offense, one is suspended.]
When one commits an offense and refuses to have it formally addressed according to the Dharma,
the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"He shall not be expelled."
This person does not believe in the existence of the substance of evil karma;
this is called the "view of causelessness" (*ahetudṛṣṭi*), for which the formal act of suspension (*karmāvaraṇa*) is performed.

They are excluded from the assembly and do not participate in communal affairs; this is the formal act of suspension for failure to repent (*apratikarmāraṇa*). This person does not believe that karma can bring about its results.
Because their views differ, this *karman* is performed to suspend them from the community; they are excluded from communal activities.
This *karman* of suspension for not relinquishing the seven evil views is applied to one who lacks faith and whose desires and afflictions obstruct the Noble Path.
This is termed "wrong view"; having performed this *karmavācanā*, he is expelled from the assembly and excluded from communal monastic affairs.
The first four types of *karmavācanā* are for disciplining those who lack proper conduct.
The final three *karmas* (formal ecclesiastical acts) treat those who lack faith.
Regarding those who lack practice, it is said they act without internal protection or external protection.
Within internal practice, there is the treatment of censure for failing to protect the community’s reliance, and the treatment of failing to protect one's own conduct.
Regarding external protection:

for those who have been expelled, it causes laypeople who have not yet developed faith to develop it; for those who have already developed faith, it causes it to increase. It also prevents those who have not yet arrived from coming.
Therefore, there are four types of *karmavācanā*.
Regarding the three types of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*):

one who does not believe in the Truth of Accumulation (*samudayasatya*) obstructs the path through the substance of their karma and is able to bring about the retribution of suffering; hence, there are two types of suspension—namely, for those who do not see [the fault] and for those who do not repent.
Because afflictions act as conditions and aids, one does not abandon even a single [unwholesome] impulse.
If this accumulation is not severed, it will still result in the retribution of suffering;
if suffering is not extinguished, there is no way out.
Since he does not seek cessation,
he is of no use within the path that deviates from the training; therefore,
one performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to suspend him.
These seven *karmas* are the methods for disciplining people.
If they do not accept punishment, one should discipline them as one would a wild horse:
driving them away once and forth is what is meant by "ordering them out. If one is to perform a *karman*, one must first possess three conditions.

First, one action is to point out the transgression; second, one is to remind them, saying, "Do you not know for yourself that you possess these three? You are subject to such-and-such an offense. Question:
Why is the *karmavācanā* procedure not performed with the threefold announcement (*tri-śrāvaṇa*)? Answer:
Matters that are easy are accomplished by a single announcement (*jñapti*) for the assembly of white-robed laypeople.
Matters that involve slight difficulty require one announcement and one motion (*jñapti-karman*), which is sufficient.
Among matters, those that are most difficult require three motions following the announcement.
In the *dhvajaka* (banner) *karmavācanā*, the difficulty or ease of the matter to be consulted and decided upon does not change.
These three [procedures] are complete; with these three, the ritual action and its meaning are sufficient.
Therefore, there is no need for the *jñapti-trivācanā* or the *jñapti-pañcavācanā*.
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, thirty-five matters are forfeited.
The Vinaya text explains this in detail: "The day has already passed.
5. The Procedure for the Recitation of the Precepts (*Poṣadha*). Regarding the fifth [section], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
There are two kinds of poṣadha.
The fourteenth-day poṣadha is called the minor poṣadha;
the twenty-fifth-day poṣadha is the major one.
