Regarding the intermediate *poṣadha*:
if a dispute arises among the bhikṣus before much time has passed,
they should reconcile and perform the *jñapti* (formal motion) alone.
The *Poṣadha* is recited at an improper time;
because the preceding day has already passed and the succeeding day has not yet arrived, it is called the "intermediate" period. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
If the eight difficult circumstances arise or other conditions warrant, the brief recitation of the precepts is permitted.
If one wishes to recite the precepts briefly,
one should first perform the single formal motion (*jñapti*).
This is followed by a brief exposition.
However, because there are difficulties regarding distance and proximity,
there are fifteen types of brief exposition of the precepts.
First, having recited the introduction,
the others proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
These are the four *pārājika* rules which the Saṃgha constantly recites;
even so it is with the seven methods for settling disputes.
Having recited the four matters of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra a second time,
the rest is announced for the monks to hear.
Having recited the four matters and the thirteen matters of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra a third time—
The others chant "The Sangha constantly hears.
Having finished reciting the fourfold introduction and the two indeterminate rules.
The others chant "The Sangha constantly hears.
When the five recitations of the introduction and the thirty matters have been completed.
The others chant, "The Sangha has heard.
Regarding the second set of five [requirements]:
first, having recited the introduction and the four matters.
The others chant, "The Saṃgha hears this constantly.
This continues until the fifth section, after the ninety matters have been recited,
whereupon the others again chant, "The Saṃgha hears this constantly."
Regarding the third set of five types:
once the introduction has been recited and the thirteen matters have been concluded,
the remainder is proclaimed as "the Sangha's constant hearing."
These constitute fifteen types of abbreviated recitation of the precepts.
Regarding the eight difficult circumstances:
the first is the difficulty of kings.
Second, thieves;
third, water;
fourth, fire.
Five diseases,
six humans,
and seven non-humans.
Regarding the eight venomous insects and other such conditions:
when the great assembly has gathered, there is a shortage of seats and bedding.
If there are many people,
or if the covering over the seats is incomplete,
or if it rains.
Either because the night of the *poṣadha* ceremony has already passed long,
or because they have been discussing the *Abhidharma*,
or because they have been preaching the Dharma until the morning stars were about to appear, one must not remain overnight [without having performed the ritual].
Regarding the enjoyment of sensual desires, whether they are near or far, it may be explained in detail.
To explain them in detail when one ought not to do so incurs an offense;
likewise, to fail to explain them briefly when one ought to do so also incurs an offense.
The same applies to difficulties during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and other such circumstances.
Furthermore, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one should ascertain whether any guests have arrived and their number,
as well as whether they are of the same or different status.
Furthermore, one should understand that whether or not [faults] are mentioned—
such as when announcing purity (*pārisuddhi*) and so forth— all should be known accordingly.
Moreover, it is said that the *śīla-dharma* (precepts) are pure.
If a bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta* offense and does not repent it, he shall not be permitted to listen to the precepts, nor shall he be permitted to serve as the reciter of the precepts;
how much less so if he has committed a grave offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says:
If one forgets [the precepts] when it is time to recite them,
the Buddha said:
"It is permitted for a bystander to provide them."
If one still forgets, they should be permitted to receive the instruction again.
If after receiving it up to three times they still forget, another person should be appointed to continue the recitation; the subsequent recitation should not be repeated.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, having received the consent (*chanda*), departed for outside the boundary.
If one intends to cause another's Dharma-affairs to fail,
the Buddha said that if they succeed, the offender commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
A bhikṣu may receive instruction from a bhikṣuṇī,
but he must not recite [the scriptures] for her;
the same applies to a bhikṣuṇī.
There are four kinds of poṣadha:
first, the three-word poṣadha;
second, the pure poṣadha.
The third is the *poṛātimokkha* (Prātimokṣa) *uposatha*;
the fourth is the *pavāraṇā* *uposatha*. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* asks:
"What is meant by *uposatha*?"
Poṣadha means abandoning all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
abandoning all afflictions and craving for existence,
and realizing the ultimate Brahma-conduct of the pure dharmas.
Therefore, it is called *poṣadha*. 6.
Regarding the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and the method for receiving extra days as clarified in the four *nikāya* vinayas: the sixth [section], the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, states:
There are five ways of upholding the Vinaya.
First, reciting from the introduction of the Prātimokṣa up to the thirty rules constitutes the first way of upholding the Vinaya.
Second, reciting the ninety rules.
Third, to recite the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* in detail;
fourth, to recite the precepts of both divisions (*bhikṣu* and *bhikṣuṇī*) in detail;
fifth, to recite the entire *Vinaya* in its entirety.
During the two seasons of spring and winter, one should reside with the first four types of *vinayadhara*;
failing to do so incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one must reside with the fifth type of *vinayadhara*.
If one does not rely on [the proper procedure], it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the rules for the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), if one arrives at the residence before the dawn of the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the "prior retreat" (*purimikā*) is established.
The period from the seventeenth day of the fourth month to the sixteenth day of the fifth month is called the "latter retreat" (*paścima-varṣā*).
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one must attend the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day.
Those who obtain the earlier *anvārambhaṇa* (rainy-season retreat) shall observe it; those who do not reach it shall observe the later *anvārambhaṇa*.
In the case of an intercalary fourth month, those observing the earlier *anvārambhaṇa* complete their term after one hundred and twenty days.
In the intercalary seventh month, those who observe the later retreat (paścima-varṣā) complete their full one hundred and twenty days.
In the intercalary fifth month, both those who observe the earlier and later retreats complete their full one hundred and twenty days. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If a bhikṣu traveling on a journey does not undertake the rains retreat (varṣā) on the day for the commencement of the *pūrvavārṣika* (first half of the rainy season),
he commits one offense of violating the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga*) upon reaching his place of residence.
If one does not enter the rains retreat on the day for the later retreat, one commits two offenses against the Vinaya.
Such a person has broken the retreat and shall not receive the distribution of robes. Thus it was asked.
This person has not entered the rains retreat.
By what statement is it broken?
Answer:

It is called "breaking" because one fails to perform the formal act of binding [the retreat] that ought to be performed. Next is the matter of "breaking the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat)," which refers to cases where the *varṣā* is not broken according to the proper procedure. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Due to circumstances involving difficult events, the *varṣā* is in all such cases not broken."

Regarding "difficulties," this refers to dangers from kings, thieves, water, fire, non-humans, malevolent beasts, and venomous insects; these are life-threatening perils and perils to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Even down to the perils posed by ants and bedbugs, it is permitted to break the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and depart.
There is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who,
during the rainy season retreat, received coarse food that was insufficient.
Not knowing what to do,
he reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
Hearing these circumstances, breaking the *anvāgama* (rainy-season retreat) is without offense.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
At that time, there was a bhikṣu...
During the period of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), one must not consume food or medicine at will,
nor employ others as one pleases.
[The monks] reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there are such matters that are contrary to one's wishes,
you are permitted to speak on account of those matters."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who observed the rains retreat in dependence upon a cowherd.
The Buddha said:
It is permitted.
If, during the rains retreat (*varṣā*), one moves to follow where a cowherd goes, it is permitted to depart.
It is likewise permitted for those who travel by boat, travelers, oil-pressers, and woodcutters to enter the rains retreat in such circumstances.
There was a bhikṣu who entered the rains retreat in dependence upon a village.
During the retreat, that village was divided into two factions.
In whatever place all necessary provisions are fully supplied, if one moves away from there, the following explains the method for receiving [the precepts] on the day of the fourfold division.
Regarding the matters of the day of receiving [the precepts]: [text follows].
In total, there are twenty-five items, ranging from detailed to brief:
matters concerning the Three Jewels, invitations from donors,
the *poṣadha* ceremony, requisites, and dwellings.
The five assemblies requested him to perform acts such as repentance, the expiation of offenses, and the reception of the full precepts;
meanwhile, an unbelieving high minister invited him,
desiring to meet with him.
Whether it be beneficial or not beneficial, one should listen to and receive the Dharma daily.
An upāsaka who has faith and joy may invite [the teacher],
or there may be some urgent matter.
If one receives the day-off for the sake of gain and offerings,
yet does not believe the invitation from one's parents who wish to see them, [one may accept].
If one receives permission to visit on a specific day, one should instruct them so that they may give rise to faith and joy.
Regarding invitations from parents:
whether for the sake of illness, distress, or matters of benefit, one may receive such permission.
The same applies to cases involving brothers, sisters, relatives, acquaintances, or former teachers and preceptors who have privately associated with a monastery.
A bhikṣu may also go for a day to seek companions for reciting the sixteen kinds of sūtras or to receive instruction.
There was a person of no faith who seized the robes and requisites of a bhikṣu,
or caused him various forms of harm;
[the bhikṣu] wished to go and inform the king.
Having received permission to depart on the day,
there was at that time a donor who invited the bhikṣus, saying:
"I wish to give alms and a dwelling," the bhikṣu thought.
"That place is too far away for me to return there on the same day."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to go for seven days;
however, you must not fail to return within those seven days."
One may receive [an item] for the sole purpose of eating on a specific day;
setting aside other causes and conditions, this includes robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and even medicinal herbs.
One must return them by the seventh day.
In this manner, one may receive permission for one day;
other matters are likewise treated as when receiving permission for seven days, fifteen days, or one month.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had received a seven-day leave to go outside the monastery boundary.
He was detained by his mother’s earnest entreaty; though he earnestly desired to return, he did not come back within the seven days.
He thought to himself, "I have failed to inform the Buddha that my year has passed," but the Buddha said,
"Your year is not lost."

If brothers and sisters have been in a private liaison from the very beginning, or if the water or land routes are cut off and so forth, not losing the [biannual] anniversary of their death is likewise [permissible]. Question:
Is it for the sake of attending to one's parents that one receives the *jñapti* (formal authorization)?
If one hears that one's parents have died, should one go [to them]? Answer:
One should not go.
One looks because one seeks survival;
now that you have no body, how can you go?
If one departs, one incurs the offense of breaking the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: Upāli asked the Buddha, "When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu is staying in a solitary place..."
When one is alone, how should one recite the precepts?
How should one receive the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*)?
How should one receive the robes?
What is the method for accepting the seven-day [allowance]? What is the seven-day medicine?
What is the universal invitation?
"What is the purification through the gift of clothing?
The Buddha said:
'I allow forest-dwelling bhikṣus to perform the poṣadha by means of mental recollection.'"
The formal act of self-indulgence (pravāraṇā) by mental reflection;
receiving a robe by mental reflection;
and receiving a seven-day period by mental reflection.
Receiving medicine through mental intention;
giving everything through mental intention;
and the total purification of robes through mental intention. Again, he asked.
Where is the seven-day period received?
The Buddha said:
"It is received within the boundary. Question:
"From whom should one receive it?
The Buddha said, "One should receive it from the fivefold assembly. He asked again.
"May one receive the seven-day [permission] through mental resolve?
The Buddha said,
"One may."
With the exception of five kinds of persons:
first, those who practice meditation in an araṇya;
second, those who dwell alone.
Third, those who have traveled far;
fourth, those who have been ill for a long time;
fifth, those who reside with their kinsmen during times of famine.
In such cases, there is no other person present to hear the mental recitation of the ritual procedure. Furthermore, it was asked:
"If a laywoman (upāsikā) wishes to go forth [into homelessness], she sends a messenger to invite a bhikṣu."
"Venerable sir, come.
I wish to go forth.
That bhikṣu then broke his summer retreat and departed.
"Should one go?
He replied, "One should go. [The questioner] asked:
If a bhikṣu is to be granted the *smṛtivinaya* or the *amūḍhavinaya*,
and a messenger is sent to summon him,
should that bhikṣu break his *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and depart?
Answer:
He should go. Again, it was asked:
"Suppose that monk, while on his way, hears that a bhikṣuṇī has died."
If one returns the precepts,
enters a non-Buddhist path,
or any one of the eight difficulties arises.
"Should one go?
He replied, "One should not go. [The questioner] asked:
If one departs [from the monastery], what offense is incurred?
Answer:

One incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, for the sake of the Three Jewels, one may accept [an invitation] for seven days, fifteen days, or one month without waiting to be summoned.
Regarding other matters, the observance of the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna* (authorization to remain for a period) is accomplished only if there is an invitation;
if there is no invitation, even if one receives it, it is not accomplished.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one may receive the seven-day and thirty-nine-night authorizations. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
One must receive the formal authorization for the Three Jewels and, having completed the task, shall return. Question:
For what reason do the days for receiving the precepts differ among the three sections? Answer:
This method of establishing the prohibitions was opened up gradually.
First they were permitted to listen for seven days;
next for fifteen days, and even up to one month,
yet the matter was still not completed.
He was granted leave for thirty-nine nights;
yet as it was still not finished, he was granted further leave until its completion, at which point he was to return.
All of this is set forth in the Vinaya.
People distinguish the distant and near according to the circumstances; thus, the rules for receiving the precepts over a period of days are scattered throughout the three divisions [of the Vinaya].
While they appear to have differences, in reality, they are no different. Question:
Question: For what reason is it that only matters concerning the Three Jewels may be accepted as completed matters, while other matters are not permitted? Answer:
Because matters concerning the Three Jewels are weighty, they are permitted.
Other matters were not permitted because they were either light or heavy;
this matter, however, was both lax and urgent.
To say it was lax means that the business was not yet completed.
Even if one does not return for the summer retreat during the course of it, there is no offense.
Regarding what is called "urgency": it refers to when affairs in the interim have been concluded.
Furthermore, if one privately refuses to return [the robe] beyond the limit, one incurs the offense of breaking the summer retreat;
therefore, it is said to be "urgent. Question:
Some say that if one does not receive the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary at the time of the initial *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one violates the summer retreat (*varṣā-bheda*).
How is this matter to be understood? Answer:
This person is unskilled in the precepts and speaks thus falsely. Why is this?
The Noble One established the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat);
one breaks the summer only by staying overnight outside.
How can it be said that the retreat is broken by merely going out for a short time?
If, during the early summer, there is no occasion for travel,
although one has received the seven-day permission, it does not constitute a valid reception of the days.
Later, if there is business, one must not go outside the boundary without receiving the days again.
Question: May one receive the seven-day leave for the purpose of begging for the three robes while staying overnight during the breaking of the summer retreat? Answer:
This is not a valid cause or condition for receiving the [seven-day] leave.
Even if the reception [of the rains retreat] is not accomplished, one still breaks the summer retreat. Question: Some say:
Regarding the statement that "one who has received the *caturvarga* [formal act] may receive it again for seven days," how is this to be understood? Answer:
This person’s reflection on the text was not careful.

The *Caturvargika-vinaya* simply states that one who receives the seven-day leave at the very end may travel for seven days during the summer retreat if there is a necessary reason; having received this seven-day leave,
he returns by the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and his failure to return on that date clarifies that his summer retreat has not been broken.
It is not a case of receiving [the *saptāha-ka*] again. Question:

If a person, for the sake of making a living, falsely claims to be a monk, or receives the seven-day [period] and so forth, and after the matter is concluded, gives a small amount of goods to the Saṃgha.
Question: Is it permissible to accept [the offerings] on that day? Answer:
This person is actually acting for his own private benefit;
he merely uses the pretext of acting for the sake of the Saṃgha.
One incurs an offense of wrong speech.
Even if one were to give away entirely all that is gained from managing one's livelihood to the community of monks,
one would still be guilty of breaking the summer retreat.
How much more so when one gives even a small amount; one’s aspiration will not be frustrated. Question:
May a bhikṣuṇī receive [the precepts] during the summer retreat? Answer:
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
For bhikṣuṇīs, there is no formal ritual (karmavācanā) for receiving an extension of the [rainy season] retreat period.
If, during the summer retreat, the senior monk upon whom they depend dies or renounces the path,
and there is a monastery of senior monks within three yojanas;
The hearing [of the Dharma] and the delimitation of the boundary are permitted.
On the fifteenth day, one should go once to request instruction on the precepts. Question:
For those entering the later retreat (paścimikā), if the days have not yet been completed by doubling [the period], [is this permissible]?
Question: Is the summer retreat attained? Answer:
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is when double the days have not yet been completed.
"One must not count [the years] by the number of years.
It is also said:
'Two people share the same summer.'"
The "small" refers to the preceding retreat (pūrvavārṣika),
and the "large" refers to the subsequent retreat (aparavārṣika).
These continue until the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the invitation for criticism (pravāraṇā) is completed.
Those who have received the *laba* (the winter retreat) are junior;
those who have not yet completed it have not yet attained the *varṣa* (the summer retreat).
One should remain for one month below the seats of those who are junior.
Having completed the double days, he returns to sit in the upper seat.
Therefore, one whose wisdom is complete but whose days are not yet full does not obtain the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Question:
If a person who has broken the *varṣā* and a person who has completed the double days but not the full days sit in the upper seat among others...
What offense is incurred? Answer:
If one accepts the prostrations of others, one incurs immeasurable *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one acts as the presiding elder (*upasthāyaka*) and separately receives offerings, [one likewise incurs such offenses].

Regarding the calculation of the money, it constitutes a grave offense. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, within the section on the three types of offenses, it states that there are three kinds of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat).
On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, before the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇa*), this is called the "early" *vassa*.
The period from the seventeenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is called the intermediate *varṣā* (intermediate retreat).
The period from the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the appearance of the dawn light is called the later *varṣā* (later retreat).
At the beginning of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should first perform four matters: first, the dissolution of the boundary;
second, the establishment of the boundary;
third, the distribution of rooms and bedding.
Regarding the fourth point, the formal entry into the rains retreat (*varṣā-pravāraṇā*): at that time,
there was a bhikṣu who wished to enter the retreat at a certain residence,
but there was no person upon whom he could rely.
There being no white-clad person present,
one falsely does not form the intention to dwell in retreat and harbors doubt,
not knowing whether the retreat has been successfully established.
He went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If one has come for the sake of the rains retreat (varṣā), the retreat is thereby established."
Upon the conclusion of the rains retreat (varṣā), five matters are to be performed: first, the dissolution of the boundary;
second, the re-establishment of the boundary;
third, the distribution of rooms and bedding.
4. The Invitation (Pravāraṇā).
5. The Inquiry Regarding the Acceptance of the Kaṭhina Cloth. Question:
What offense does one who has broken the rainy-season retreat incur? Answer: [The following].
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Failing to enter the earlier retreat is a *duṣkṛta*;
failing to enter the later retreat is a *pāyattika*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
There are five types of persons who may not receive the robe for the rainy season retreat (*varṣāśāṭī*):
first, one who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*);
second, one who has broken the summer retreat (*chinnasīmā*).
Third, those who do not practice the way;
fourth, death;
fifth, failing to give instructions before passing away.
Regarding the minor transgressions of one who has broken the summer retreat: first, they are rebuked by all the Buddhas;
second, they are rebuked by devas and worldly people;
third, they have violated the summer retreat.
Fourth, one incurs an offense;
fifth, one is not permitted to receive the *guṇa-cīvara*;
sixth, one is not permitted to receive the five types of benefits.
Seventh, one shall not receive offerings.
Eighth, one shall not receive robes or requisites for the rainy season retreat.
Ninth, an evil reputation shall spread.
Tenth: Regretting [one's actions] later leads to rebirth in hell.
7. The Procedure for the *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Indulgence). Regarding the seventh section on the *Pravāraṇā* procedure, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
Those who have entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣa*) should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Those who observe the later retreat perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
If those who observe the earlier and later retreats are in the same location,
they should follow the *pravāraṇā* of those who observed the earlier retreat.
The procedure for the *pārivāsika* (probationary) monks to observe the *pravāraṇā* together with others: if there are five persons, they perform the *pravāraṇā* in full detail;
if there are four, three, or two persons, they perform the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face.
One person performs the *pravāraṇā* through mental intention and verbal expression. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"At the time of the *pravāraṇā*, two persons shall be appointed;
three persons or one person may not be appointed."
One who is internally endowed with the five virtues shall act as the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) officiant for the Saṃgha.
The five virtues are:
not acting out of favoritism, fear, or delusion; knowing whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not yet performed; and asking [questions regarding these matters].
For what reason are two persons appointed together for the *pravāraṇā*, rather than three or one? Answer:
If only one person were appointed, he would be appointed by the Saṃgha alone.
This is called a "monk-messenger" (saṃghadūta) who is properly authorized to charge others with offenses;
however, if this person themselves has an offense,
there is no one who may charge them.
Therefore, two persons must be appointed.
When accusing someone of an offense, each person must speak individually;
they may not do so simultaneously.
Therefore, there must not be fewer than three persons. Question:
What is the dharma called *pravāraṇā*? Answer:
*Pravāraṇā* is the dharma for the raising of charges.
This was originally due to raising charges during the summer retreat,
which caused discord and strife among the assembly;
therefore, it was suspended.
Upon reaching summer, they do not share common utensils;
rather, they confess their offenses to one another to achieve purity.
Thereafter, they act according to circumstances. Question: [What follows?]
Question: For what reason must confession necessarily be prompted by another person?
Answer: Because most people are deluded regarding themselves;
it is clear that if one does not recognize one's own transgressions, there is no way to achieve repentance; therefore, it is necessary for another to prompt one. Question:
People say that the *pravāraṇā* is the ritual for concluding the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
How should one answer this?
This explanation is not in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because if one were to untie what was originally bound, one would immediately lose the summer retreat.
Therefore, it is known that this is not a practice of the summer retreat. Question:
Some say that *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) is a dharma of relinquishment.
Furthermore, how is this so? Answer:
This statement is incorrect.
If *pravāraṇā* were a dharma of relinquishment, [it would follow that one could not perform it].
One should abandon the commission of transgressions. Why, then, say:
"If I see my fault, I shall confess it according to the Dharma"?
Therefore, know that this is incorrect.
If difficult circumstances arise at the time of the *pravāraṇā*,
it is permitted to perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) and then each person together perform the *pravāraṇā* with three utterances.
Regarding the difficulties, as clarified in the explanation of the *śīla* (precepts),
there are five ways of giving consent (*chanda*).
One word, "giving consent," establishes the act of giving consent.
Second, he speaks of desire for my sake;
third, he manifests bodily signs;
fourth, he speaks with his voice.

The five ways of manifesting through bodily appearance and verbal expression are the same as those for giving the *chanda* (consent) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. There are five ways that the *chanda* is lost: first, the death of the bhikṣu who received the *chanda*;
second, his renunciation of the religious life (*pravrajyā*).
Third, entering among the assemblies of non-Buddhists;
fourth, going among the monks of other sects;
fifth, arriving at the preeminence of the precepts.

8. The Method for Robes as Clarified in the Vinayas and Treatises of the Four Schools. The eighth section on the method for robes as clarified in the Vinayas and treatises of the four schools concerns the three robes and six requisites.
First is the *antarvāsa*, which is here called the five-strip robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*).
One long, one short, and one heavy;
these are used for wearing within the monastery,
as well as when walking on the path or during the various periods of walking meditation.
It is worn when sewing robes, washing alms bowls, or performing various tasks. Second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, this seven-strip robe,
which consists of two long pieces and one short piece, doubled in thickness,
and is constructed by cutting the fabric into strips.
One wears it when entering an assembly,
when preaching the Dharma, during the morning and evening meals,
and when walking in meditation or performing prostrations; this robe is called the *saṃghāṭī*, or the "many-stripped" robe.
It is also called the "Great Assembly" (Mahāsaṃgha).
It is worn when entering royal palaces or villages, when subduing Māras, following the path, or converting wicked people;
its great dignity inspires awe in both [gods and humans] and causes living beings to develop faith and reverence. The *pātra* (alms bowl) is made of either clay or iron.
The large [vessel] holds three *sheng*;
the small holds one and a half *sheng*.
One should receive the infused oil according to the Dharma without [the recipient] physically touching it.
Those who constantly use five *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) should know that the small ones are three feet in width and four feet in length at most;
the large ones are five feet in length at most.
It is four chi wide;
its four borders are dyed in a discolored hue. It has six needle-cases made of copper, iron, tin, bamboo, wood, or other materials.
Its use is according to one's personal needs.
Regarding the five robes of a bhikṣuṇī:
these include the two additional robes, the *saṃkakṣikā* and the *saṃghāṭī*. Question:
How many factors must be fulfilled for the three robes to be properly received and maintained according to the Dharma? Answer: [As follows].
One who possesses four qualities is said to have received and maintained [the precepts] in accordance with the Dharma;
one who does not possess these four qualities has not achieved such reception and maintenance. What are these four?
First, the substance of the wealth is in accordance with the Dharma;
second, the dyeing of the color is in accordance with the Dharma;
third, the manufacture is in accordance with the Dharma.
The four measures are in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by "the substance of wealth being in accordance with the Dharma"?

Fine silk, raw silk, cotton cloth, and so forth—provided they are not items subject to forfeiture for transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) and are not items for trade—are called "in accordance with the Dharma."
If materials such as *liáng*, *luó*, *qǐ*, *gǔ*, *shā*, or *xiè* are coarse, they do not constitute valid possession (*dhāraṇa*).
How, then, is dyeing performed according to the Dharma?
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
The five primary colors cannot be accepted or maintained:
first, true blue;
second, true yellow.
If they are truly red,
truly white, truly black,
and so forth, they do not constitute valid acceptance and observance.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"This true purple, saffron, turmeric, *nāgakesara*, and the color of *campaka* flowers are also called 'non-dharma colors' (*adharmavarṇa*).
What, then, is called a 'dharma color' (*dharmavarṇa*)?"
Answer:
All the Vinayas state that among the three kinds of colors, one may alter them as one pleases.
If it is blue, black, or madder-colored,
it is called "in accordance with the Dharma.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
It is permitted to destroy natural colors and fine cotton garments so that they may be accepted and maintained;
however, the dharma of a bhikṣu requires that one must certainly abandon ornaments and finery,
and rest from conceit while practicing the Way.
Even now, they remain attached to fine colors, indulging in the defilements of passion and arrogance;
failing to eliminate these, they delight in the path while remaining aloof and simple,
thereby provoking the derision of the laity.
This damages the Buddha-dharma.
How can this be considered acting in accordance with the Dharma?
Instead, one should use a hooked needle to pierce the four edges and attach loops and fasteners at the corners.
The five strips consist of one long and one short;
whether they are cut or uncut, they all constitute valid possession through formal acceptance.
The seven-strip robe consists of two long strips and one short strip;
it must be made by means of cutting.
There are nine grades of the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*); this is according to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*. The lowest grade is as follows:
Those with nine, eleven, or thirteen strips should have two long and one short;

There was a bhikṣu who put on his robe inside out; when he entered the water, it became soaked and rotted within the folds.
The Buddha said:

during non-rainy weather, it is as one pleases.
There was a bhikṣu.

Next, the method for receiving [the robes] when they have been lost, and the method for receiving [them] so that they are not lost, is explained.
The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If the three robes are torn, regardless of the size of the holes, as long as the seams remain unbroken, they constitute valid possession."

The seven-strip outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) has a width of eight finger-breadths; if it is worn inside [the inner robe], its formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is not lost.

The four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) are also called the four noble lineages (*catvāra āryavaṃśāḥ*). First, relying on rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla-cīvara*); this person is of superior grade.
To discard precious objects and take them as clothing,
rather than accepting offerings of faith—
this is the least of desires.
One who merely obtains enough for their own body to cultivate the Way already possesses a different purpose [from others].
A person of middle capacity cannot endure listening to [discourses on] robes, nor can they receive the same shared property as those in the monastic order.

Those of inferior capacity listen to and accept separate alms and expensive, worn-out robes; those of superior capacity, relying on the method of begging, eliminate pride and craving, and beg for food while subduing their bodies.
To obtain the means for sustaining the body and supporting life while practicing the Path;
those of middle capacity listen to the teachings and receive the succession of offerings from the Sangha, as well as providing offerings themselves.
Those of inferior capacity listen to and receive the Sangha’s regular meals and special invitations for offerings; those of superior capacity sit upon grass under trees.
They dwell among burial mounds, beneath trees, in secluded places, or by the side of roads, minimizing their attachments.
Those of middle capacity are permitted to receive rooms according to the monastic order, as well as small huts sufficient for the body and long-haired bedding.
Those of lower capacity are permitted to receive separate rooms, halls, pavilions, couches, seats, woolen rugs, and quilts.
Such matters as these constitute the four reliances on putrid medicines. When persons of superior capacity are ill, they take these aged and fermented substances to eliminate karmic obstacles;
indeed, the liquid from excrement and urine can cure all manner of diseases.
One should not harm others;

rather, one should take only what cures illness in order to preserve the body for the practice of the Way. Those of middle capacity receive ghee, oil, and honey according to the sequence of the Saṃgha;
those of lower capacity receive individual offerings from bhikṣus.
It is recorded that these four dharmas provide the sustenance for the body and livelihood, ensuring a state of peace.
The monastic robes serve as external sustenance,
while the ten [precepts] serve as internal sustenance.
Requisites for bedding ward off external afflictions;
medicinal decoctions eliminate internal afflictions.
For the former, one relies upon clothing and dwellings.
Internally relying on food and medicine,
one must have these four conditions to cultivate the Path.
Because these four dharmas can give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called the Four Noble Lineages (*catur-ārya-vaṃśa*).
A bhikṣu should practice in accordance with his own capacity and rely upon it;
he must not cultivate practices that exceed his limits. Why is this?
If a person of superior capacity practices the dharmas of an inferior person, they will regress;
if a person of inferior capacity practices the dharmas of a superior person, they will not even equal those of the middling person.
Since superior dharmas are transcendent, one must each accord with one's own strength and cultivate the path with a diligent mind.
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika* says:
"If you wish to attain the bliss of quiescence,
you should study the dharma of the śramaṇa."
If one ceases [activity], one sustains body and life,
like a snake entering a mouse hole;
thus one may obtain the bliss of quiescence.
One should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa;
clothing and food are merely for sustaining the body and life,
while one should apply oneself with diligence in accordance with the community.
Desiring to attain the bliss of tranquility,
one should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa;
having known all, one is fully satisfied.

9. The Kaṭhina Robe. Regarding the ninth [chapter], the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: Question:
How many people may obtain the kaṭhina robe?
Answer: [As follows].
Down to a group of five persons, one may undertake the prior *anvārambhaṇa* (early) retreat and the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* (late) retreat.
Those who have broken the retreat and those who reside in a separate dwelling place are not permitted to undertake them.
If the number of residents at a dwelling place does not reach five,
it is permissible to summon monks from another monastery to complete the quorum for the formal act;
however, guest monks may not be so summoned.
If there are four *bhikṣus* and one *śrāmaṇera* at a residence,
and the summer retreat is about to end, the *śrāmaṇera* who wishes to receive the full precepts may do so with five persons present.
It is the same if there are four *śrāmaṇeras* and one *bhikṣu*.

If there are five persons at a residence, or more than five, who do not understand how to accept the *guṇavat-cīvara*, they may invite a person from another monastery who knows the Dharma to perform the *karmavācanā*; they themselves may not accept it. Question.
Question: Whose robes may be used to make a *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha? Answer:
The robes of the seven classes of followers, as well as those of devas and humans, may be accepted and made into a *kaṭhina* robe.
If someone who does not understand how to make a *kaṭhina* robe comes to inquire about it...
A bhikṣu should be instructed;
whether it be a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, or an antarvāsaka,
he may accept each robe as it is made.
If a person offers many *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robes),
one should accept only one robe;
the remainder should be distributed.
This *kaṭhina* robe should be formally assigned (*karmavācanā*) to a monk whose robes are worn out;
if there are many monks with worn-out robes, it should be given to one who is old among those with worn-out robes,
or to one whose robes are most tattered.
One must not give [the robe] to those who are stingy, stubborn, or greedy. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The *kaṭhina* robe refers to a new garment that has been formally accepted as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Once it has been given away through the rite of pure donation (*śuddha-dāna*), one obtains the merit (*guṇa*) of the *kaṭhina*."
One may obtain the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe),
the *saṃghāṭī*, the *saptaka*, the *pañcaka*, the *vraṇapracchādaka*, and the *varṣāśāṭī*.
These various robes, however, have never been used by the *kaurava*.
All may then make the *kaṭhina* robe.
The Buddha said:
"It is not merely by measurement that one is said to receive the *kaṭhina* robe."
Not only stained,
not only settled upon its object,
and not only pressed down at the four corners.
It is not merely because it has leaves, nor is it merely because it is embroidered with pins; thus it is called the "robe of received merit.
If one makes it from old or tattered cloth, [it is still so called].
If it is not prepared by the Saṃgha;
if it is dyed the color of saffron;
or if it has been kept overnight.
If one does not receive it with a mind fixed in concentration,
if one does not perform it with purity,

If it is not made by cutting and piecing,
or if it is made from cloth other than that of the five classes of robes,
it is not called "receiving the *kaṭhina* robe. According to the *Kaṭhina-vidhi* in twenty-seven fascicles, once the *kaṭhina* robe has been received, one obtains five kinds of benefits.
First, one may keep an extra robe for more than ten days without performing the ritual of *paryāpanna*.

Third, receiving food from a separate group;

fourth, eating successive meals (turning back to eat after having left); fifth, entering a village before or after a meal without having announced one’s intention, when there is already an invitation elsewhere during the morning period—this refers to visiting other households without announcing one’s departure. These five matters are likewise permitted for one month during the *kārttika* month. The *kārttika* month is the month for making robes (*cīvara*).
From the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month,

The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time praise and authorize it.

The bhikṣu said,

"One should not discard it because it cannot be drunk.
The Buddha said,

Discard a small amount of water from the top;
the pure water below should be drunk.
If there is a small amount of food at the bottom of the water, it should be treated in the same way.
Taking the bowl, he took water from the pond;

The Buddha said,

11. On the Rules for the Community Living Together and the Investigation of Monks. Chapter Eleven: Since monastic affairs are grave, managing them is no easy task.
Were it not for one whose virtuous conduct is fully realized within and who possesses both majesty and capability— whose mind is humble and who does not shrink from toil—
how could one discern the heterodox and manage affairs?
If one succeeds, there is the benefit of ascending to heaven;
if one fails, there is the loss that follows from before.
This applies to all who adjudicate legal matters as well as those who manage the Three Jewels.
One must clearly understand the sutras and vinaya,
act in accordance with the principles,
and neither exalt oneself nor disparage others.
He does not encroach upon others' property;
once he has fulfilled his duties, he seeks no reward or gratitude,
nor does he pursue fame or reputation.
If one can thus directly protect the Triple Gem,
the merit of benefiting oneself and others will be inexhaustible.
This applies to those who adjudicate disputes.
One should be endowed with five virtues:
first, maintaining pure precepts with a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, never distorting the principles;
second, being widely learned, clear-sighted, and abiding in the understanding of the Vinaya.

First, his principles are difficult to refute; second, he extensively recites the two sets of precepts and possesses a keen understanding of their relative gravity; third, he is capable of both questioning and answering;
and fourth, he is able to provide instruction and reprimand according to the Dharma, as well as carry out formal acts of expulsion.

To cause others to attain joy, to be capable of evaluating what is appropriate, to be skilled in the five types of wholesome conduct that can extinguish disputes arising from deficiencies, and to be adept in skillful means so as to eliminate the stains of prior matters—one who possesses these five virtues is fit to manage the affairs of the Saṃgha;
such are the virtues of a Great Man.
When wishing to resolve the affairs of others, one should first examine five factors:
first, observe whether the matter at hand is true; second, observe whether it will be beneficial in the future.
The third observation is whether it is appropriate for the time;
the fourth observation is whether it will not cause the Saṃgha to give rise to defilement;
the fifth observation is whether it can be properly resolved.
Having observed these five dharmas in succession, one should give rise to wholesome thoughts and speech.

When the assembly establishes regulations to punish and govern evil persons and to adjudicate matters, the Buddha said: "A *vinayadhara* (master of discipline) who judges cases for others must be endowed with five virtues."
First, skillfully knowing the characteristics of transgressions;
second, skillfully knowing the characteristics of non-transgressions;
third, skillfully knowing the characteristics of light offenses.
Fourth, one must well understand the gravity of the matter.
Fifth, one must well understand how to reach a definitive judgment without doubt.

One who abides in the Vinaya without wavering and possesses these five virtues may then adjudicate matters for others; a person who brings charges against another must likewise internally possess these five virtues.

First, knowing the proper time: one does not engage with the assembly at an inappropriate time; when it is appropriate to raise a matter, one should do so at the right moment, using coarse words of Dharma to admonish and instruct. Second, possessing a compassionate mind: one does not harbor thoughts of anger, but intends to benefit others rather than incite resentment. If one does not reflect upon these five dharmas, [one will fail].
One must not frivolously speak of the faults of others;
doing so may disturb the monastic community or cause distress to oneself and others.
The temple master and the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) should be endowed with five virtues.

First, one should not harbor partiality toward kin; second, one should not feel resentment or seek retribution against enemies; third, one should not be terrified or afraid of the powerful; fourth, one should not be deluded or arrogant toward the wise; fifth, one should know one's own lot and, when it has not yet been assigned, be skillful in determining one's place so as to bring harmony to the hearts of the assembly. When entering an assembly, one should be endowed with these five virtues.
First, one should act with a mind of loving-kindness; if one treats the assembly with arrogance, it will cause the assembly to be displeased.

Therefore, one must first win the affection of the assembly through the Dharma before entering. Second, one should humble oneself, using a cloth for wiping dust, maintaining a mind of humility, being careful regarding transgressions, and not treating the assembly with pride or contempt. Third, one should know the proper manner of sitting and rising.
If one sees a senior elder (sthavira), one should not sit down;
if one sees a junior elder (navaka), one should not stand up, for the assembly must remain composed. When among the Sangha, one should not engage in miscellaneous talk or discuss worldly matters.

Whether one preaches the Dharma oneself or requests another to preach it, the assembly relies upon the Dharma. Fifth, if one sees something improper within the Saṃgha and cannot endure it in one's heart, one should remain silent;
there are five kinds of improper silence that do not involve the initiation of quarrels or disputes.
First, if the *karmavācanā* is performed according to the Dharma but the minds are not in accord,
one may remain silent and acquiesce while participating in the ritual proceedings; yet, if one's views differ,
it is permissible to voice one's objections, even if the underlying dispositions remain discordant.
1. This causes the communal dharma to fail. 2. If one obtains companions who share the same intent, one should not remain silent and tolerate it;
a virtuous person who assists oneself should not silently endure what is contrary to the Dharma. 3. If one sees a minor offense...
If one remains silent and allows the matter to be extinguished, yet tolerates a defiled assembly, the Sangha shall impose a *parivāsa* (probation) upon him;
this is called "separate dwelling" (*pārivāsika*). If the Sangha, while remaining silent, performs the three formal acts of accusation, it is termed "separate dwelling."

One must not participate in the same ritual act as them; even if one is present on the boundary of the *sīmā* (precept field), if one remains silent while a *karmavācanā* is about to be performed, one should call out for those who have gathered to assemble.
Fearing that the assembly might be incomplete and thus constitute a separate group (*nānāsaṃgha*), there are five kinds of lawful silence.
1. When one witnesses another performing an illegal act, it is reasonable to silently stop that illegal *karmavācanā* (formal procedure) by means of censure;
however, this is not the same as remaining silent when one has no fault oneself, for fear that doing so at an inappropriate time might disturb the minds of the assembly.

2. If one lacks companions and remains silent while alone, such speech would be useless, as the assembly is already in opposition. 3. If one commits a grave offense and remains silent while initiating a major matter, there is a danger that it may cause disorder within the assembly. 4. While living together, one should remain silent in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony, allowing no room for dissent. 5. While living together, once all members have assembled, it is improper to cause discord or confusion through silence.

12. The Meaning of the Property of the Triple Gem as Clarified in the Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries. Section Twelve: On the Meaning of the Property of the Triple Gem as Clarified in the Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries. The property of the Triple Gem is of great importance and must not be treated with negligence.
If one employs [the property] with propriety, one accords with the teachings and achieves goodness;
if one wastes it without moderation, one violates principle and incurs transgression.
Those who wish to understand the matter of the Three Jewels' property in detail:
One must penetrate deeply into the characteristics of the precepts and recognize their gravity;
only by maintaining a reverent mind and fearing transgression can one be entrusted with these duties.
If one does not do so, one should distance oneself from them immediately, as if avoiding a pit of fire.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu acts as the master of a monastery and the stūpa has no property, while the Saṃgha does possess property,
he then forms this thought:"
That people make offerings to the Saṃgha is entirely due to the grace of the Buddha.
If one takes property belonging to the Saṃgha to repair a stūpa, this constitutes a grave offense for the monastery’s administrator.
Conversely, if the stūpa possesses property, it may be used to make offerings to the Saṃgha.
If the Sangha has no property,
or if the Sangha possesses property while the stūpa has none,
one may lawfully borrow from those administrators for that purpose.
When lending goods, one should clearly prepare a written contract and read it before the Saṃgha so that the monks may all know of it.
If one does not read it, one commits an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vibhāṣā-āpatti).
Those items should be returned in accordance with the essential terms of the contract.
Regarding the matters of property belonging to the Sangha, there are generally five types of designations.
First, as for the property of the Sangha from the four quarters, all heavy (fixed) items are designated as "property of the Sangha from the four quarters."
From the highest level of Arhats down to the lowest level of Śrāmaṇeras, all have their share.
There is no question of combining portions, selling, lending to others, or using them for private purposes.
Why is it that one does not speak of "the property of the Sangha of the ten directions" but rather says "the four directions"? Answer: [The text continues: ... [The answer follows].
Within a single world-system, there are no monks above or below;
the term "four directions" is used broadly to encompass the four intermediate points as well as above and below.
Therefore, only the four cardinal directions are discussed.
If one speaks of the ten directions, there is likewise no hindrance;
for now, this clarifies the "peripheral" [meaning].
Regarding the second point, the property of the permanently established Sangha (*nitya-saṃghika-vastu*): as for the term "permanent," it means—
It must always remain in this place and may not be moved;
when the Saṃgha from the four directions arrives, it shall be used right here.

Because it is named after its object, it is called "property of the permanently resident Saṃgha" (sthāvarasaṃghika). Third is the property of the *caitya* Saṃgha (*caityasaṃghika*): if a layperson makes a gift of land specifically for the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present Saṃgha).
Each person built their own private dwelling,
so that when the Saṃgha from the four directions arrived, there was no place to accommodate them.
Consequently, someone built rooms and lodgings upon this private land for the sake of the Saṃgha from the four directions.
It provides all that is required.
Because this hall can attract the Saṃgha from the four quarters to assemble here, it is called "the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters" (cātuddisa-saṃgha).
Fourth is the property of the Saṃgha as a whole (saṃghika). Regarding "as a whole" (saṃghika):
This is called "the great assembly" (*mahāsangha*). Since this property belongs to the great assembly collectively, it is called "property of the *saṃgha*.
Fifth is "property of the *saṃgha*-garland": when flowers from within the *saṃgha*'s garden are used to make garlands, the resulting material value is acquired [as such].

From the present Saṃgha of the four quarters, from the Arhats above down to the śrāmaṇeras below.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

They divided the communal property of the Saṃgha into five portions,

On account of this matter, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the four directions there are five kinds of things that cannot be guarded and cannot be divided."
First, the site of the dwelling;

Whether it be guarding, selling, or dividing [the property], the offense of *sthūlātyaya* is the same as in the four-part [Vinaya];
the only difference is that it is divided into four parts. Furthermore, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:

This applies generally to all [plants]. Regarding vegetables, it is permitted to harvest them once they have been planted.

taking them gradually in this manner is also like this. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Upāli asked the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "It is permitted."

If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle items) who is sent to gather fruit from a tree to be eaten, the large timber from the four directions should be used by the Saṃgha for beams and rafters.
The bark and leaves of the tree may be used at will by the bhikṣus. If there are withered trees on the property of the Saṃgha, [they may likewise be used].

Because this belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
If there is a fine tree upon monastic land,
the community may, in harmony, use it to construct a stūpa or a monastic dwelling;
if they are not in harmony, they may not do so.

the community of monks may divide the location and grant it to them for their use.

they may use them to maintain the dwelling.

this tree need not be formally reported to the Saṃgha and may be used. However, for flowering trees and fruit trees, they must be used by the entire Saṃgha in harmony for the purpose of repairing stūpas or constructing monastic cells.
I must not break it.

"If a monastery building is empty and abandoned with no one present..."
When a bhikṣu comes or goes and sees fruit on a tree, he should strike the bell;

If a donor provides a dwelling as a gift, [one may accept it].

the value must be returned.

If, during times of famine, food and drink are difficult for the Saṃgha to obtain;
or during times of illness or civil unrest within the realm;
a bhikṣu may abandon the monastery and depart.
If one knows that the temple buildings, gardens,
and fruits have no one to oversee them, such heavy items may be used for food and drink in order to protect the dwelling place.

If a donor offers the three robes as a gift,
yet the Sangha has no rooms or quarters, [one may accept them].
If one performs a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) to divert funds for the construction of a dwelling,
and the community acts in harmony, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu serves as the official in charge of distributing rewards, [he should act accordingly].
If someone else tunnels through a wall and steals it away,
that bhikṣu has guarded it with such diligence and secured the room so firmly that,
even though it is lost, he is not required to make restitution.
If one does not guard [the property] with care, one must compensate for it all.
Thus it should be understood in detail. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says:
A bhikṣu knows that among the property of the Saṃgha there is that which should be given and that which should not be given.

it should be given either for the sake of harm or for the sake of benefit.

If one does not give them, they may burn down the monastic quarters. Although one should not give to them, fearing such damage might occur, one should give according to what is available, however much or little it may be.

If it concerns kings or those of great power, they should be granted [these things]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If I give it to him, I fear he will commit an offense;

when the bhikṣu did not give it to him, the thief cut off the bhikṣu’s waist.

"If there is such a place of fear..."
If one begs for half, give half; if one begs for little, give little;

they benefit from receiving offerings.

one then devalues the faithful offerings and commits many transgressions.
If one wishes to distribute items, let those who possess superior virtue divide them;
whether good or bad, they should be distributed equally without partiality.
The rest of the monastic community must likewise not give rise to greed.
One must not speak recklessly regarding gains and offerings, for they are difficult to digest; whether one is poor or wealthy does not depend on these.
Furthermore, do not harbor resentment or seek to alter another's aspirations and conduct.
If you obtain robes, you should only cut them into pieces.

rather, one should say:
"I should not accept this impure wealth.

One should speak thus to the attendant (kappiyakāraka):
If one knows this while looking at it,
and this person subsequently gives it back to the bhikṣu,
it shall be treated as the property of that person.

Therefore, when employing a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*), at the time one requires robes, one must seek them according to the Dharma, request them according to the Dharma, receive them according to the Dharma, accept them according to the Dharma, and use them according to the Dharma. (From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: There was a bhikṣu...)
His parents were poor and wished to make offerings;

The Fourfold Vinaya and its Commentaries clarify the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) and seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*), as well as the gravity of upholding or violating them. This concludes the fourteenth section: The person who upholds the Vinaya possesses five virtuous qualities.
First, the category of precepts is firm and stable;
second, one excels over all enemies and possesses decisive judgment within the assembly, free from doubt or fear.
Third, they are able to resolve doubts and regrets;
fourth, they skillfully uphold the Vinaya;
fifth, they cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
The Vinaya Piṭaka has four names.
The first is called *śīla* (precepts). Translated according to its teaching, it refers to the method for preventing wrongdoing;
this clarifies that these dharmas are capable of restraining the body and speech.
If one speaks in terms of the practice of the mind that restrains evil, it is called "precept" (śīla);
this clarifies that the mind is capable of ensuring that body and speech do not commit evil. These two are termed "vinaya. There are two approaches to its interpretation:
first, the teaching (śāsana).
Second, regarding conduct:
that which evaluates the gravity [of offenses] according to the teachings is called *vinaya*.
Regarding conduct, that which tames the unruly and coarse is called *vinaya*. Third, *prātimokṣa* is a term from the Western Regions (India).
In this region, it was previously translated as "liberation from this and that.
When translating according to the teachings, this is the method for untying bonds;
by relying upon it, those who have left the household life escape the fetters and obstructions of the world.
In every place and at all times, body and mind are free from entanglement;
hence it is said that "in each and every instance there is liberation.
To explain this in terms of practice, it refers to a mind that has severed its bonds.
Because within every moment of thought one is able to separate from and abandon afflictions,
it is called "liberation.
It is also termed "liberation obtained as a result of retribution" (*vipākaja-vimukti*).
This clarifies the practice of upholding the precepts.

When the practice is fulfilled, the accumulated karmic retribution naturally ceases; it is also said that one preserves liberation. It is clear that upholding the precepts with determination can certainly sever the bonds of affliction. The fourth name is *vinaya*, which is likewise a Western (Sanskrit) term.
This is translated as "cessation" (*nirodha*).
When explained according to the teaching, it is called "cessation" because this dharma is able to extinguish disputes and arguments.
In terms of practice:
severing birth and death, the exhaustion of suffering,
the unconditioned, and profound stillness constitute cessation (*nirodha*).
Among these four, the names of the first two are established based on their causes:
that which externally prevents wrongdoing is called "precept" (śīla), and that which internally accords with [the path] is called "discipline" (vinaya).
The latter two names are established based on their results.
"Liberation" refers to the state where afflictions are exhausted, which is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).
"Fruitional cessation" refers to the simultaneous extinction of both body and wisdom.
This is the fruit of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, the explanation of precepts (*śīla*) and discipline (*vinaya*) encompasses both cause and fruit.
This is the conditioned practice of transcendence;
liberation and the fruit of cessation are both causes and [the result].
This is the unconditioned departure.
Regarding these four, they are all called "piṭakas" (baskets) because they encompass the textual expressions and essential meanings of the teachings;
thus they are named "piṭakas."
Because one can give rise to manifold virtues and boundless benefit through understanding based on practice, it is called a "Piṭaka" (Treasury).
As for the five sections: first is the *Pārājika* section;
this is a transliteration of the Central Asian language (Hu-yin).
The meaning here is "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*).
If one violates this precept, one is forever cast out from the two types of ritual procedures—the *poṣadha* and the *karmavācanā*—of the pure assembly;
because one will never again have a share therein, it is called "without remainder."
The *Caturvarga-vinaya* states:
"A *pārājika* offense is like severing a person's head;
it cannot be restored."
A bhikṣu is also like this:
one who commits this offense no longer constitutes a bhikṣu;
therefore, it is called a pārājika.
It is called "falling into such a transgression.
One who commits such an extremely evil and grave offense falls immediately.
In such an unfavorable state,
one is not called a bhikṣu;
one is not of the lineage of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
Regarding the term *pārājika* as meaning "one who has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu":
it refers to one who has receded from and fallen away from the knowledge of the Dharma, such that they no longer possess a share in the fruits of the Path.
This is called *pārājika*.
Even that which is an offense such that it cannot be confessed and purified is called a *pārājika*.
Question:

Answer:
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

The Bhikṣu originally maintains the precepts with a pure mind, yet he has transgressed against the Evil Māra. This section on the two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses is a transcription of the Hu (Sogdian/Tocharian) sound;
in this [Chinese] language, it is called *sengcan* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa).
If one commits these offenses, one's conduct becomes impaired and deficient.

The number of *poṣadha* observances remains as before; because one emerges from the midst of the *karmavācanā* assembly and surpasses Māra, and because its offenses are categorized accordingly, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Regarding the term *saṃgha*, the offense belongs to the Saṃgha;
because one must undergo repentance before the Saṃgha for a residual offense (*śeṣa*), it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa means that there is a remainder to this offense;
because it must be dealt with through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*), it is called saṃghāvaśeṣa."
Furthermore, if one confesses and repents this matter before the Saṃgha,
it is likewise a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means that this offense has a remainder;
there are still causes and conditions remaining.
Those who are capable of being cured through reliance [on the Saṃgha] and may remain within the community to extinguish [the offense] are called *pāyattika*—this is a Western (Sanskrit) term;
translated here, it means "falling" (*duo*).
If one violates this precept, one falls into the three miserable realms;
because one is scorched, boiled, and obstructed, it is called "falling.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
*Pāyattika* means "burning and obstructing.
If one does not repent of one's transgression, it can obstruct this Path;
therefore, it is called *pāyattika*. The four names for *pratideśanīya* are likewise transliterations from the Western [Indic] language.
This method is called "confessing toward another.
If one has committed an offense against this precept that merits censure,
the visiting monk should listen as the offender discloses the fault and performs the face-to-face confession for its removal.
Therefore, it is said that one should repent before them. Fifth is the category of *śikṣākaraṇīya*, which in this region is called "that which should be learned.
This clarifies that these *duṣkṛta* offenses are the most minor of the transgressions concerning dignified conduct and ascetic practice.
Because it is difficult to guard and maintain, it is called "protection";
since it must be diligently practiced to achieve mastery,
it says, "one should train."
These five categories protect three types of conduct:
the first category protects fundamental conduct;
the second protects communal conduct.
The lower three [categories] protect dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Furthermore, they serve to prevent three kinds of obstacles:
the first two sections protect against the offenses that obstruct the Path.
The first category [of offenses] primarily obstructs the path of the saṃgha; the second category primarily obstructs the community.
The third category prevents the transgression of attachment and grasping;
without it, one remains submerged in the three realms of existence, having no means of deliverance.
The final two articles prevent criticism for excessive offenses;
they are intended to transform and benefit living beings,
rather than encouraging transgressions through the *pratideśanīya* rules and then requiring repentance.

The first section, "Exhortation to Focus on the Essence," urges that one must not transgress the meaning [of the precepts]. This section encompasses all chapters, clarifying them through their mutual interrelation; it discusses the five categories of precepts as its substance.
All of these take the three karmas of correct goodness as their substance.
However, offenses—whether light or heavy—are established according to circumstances and classified into five grades.
These are then systematically organized into chapters based on their common characteristics. Next, the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*) are explained;
the five chapters were explained above.
These constitute five groups.
The sixth is named *sthūlātyaya* (偷蘭聚); this is a transcription of the Hu (Indic) sound, which in this region [of China] is pronounced as "tōu-lán."
There are four types of this offense:
first, the *sthūlātyaya* of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), which entails banishment;
second, the *sthūlātyaya* of the preliminary preparations (*prayoga*) for the offenses of the first category, which must be confessed before an assembly of eight monks.

The second section on expedient means states that the four *sthūlātyaya* offenses committed independently should be confessed before a sangha of four; those committed with three people should be confessed before three individuals.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"The term *sthūlātyaya* means 'great obstruction' (*mahā-āvaraṇa*)."

To say that it obstructs the wholesome path is called a great hindrance to the path. Regarding the seventh [category], the "Collection of Evil Explanations" (pāpavāda-kalāpa), which resembles the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing):
the *Sudarsana-vinaya-śāstra* states:
*Duṣ-ṭhūla* means "evil";
*kṛcchra* means "to do";
thus, it signifies the act of doing evil.
It is also said:
"Stumbling in body is called *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
an offense of speech is called *durbhāṣita* (ill-spoken)."
Now, taking only those verbal offenses that constitute transgressions of dignified conduct (*vīryāpatha*) as the seventh category;
these two categories of offenses—
If one commits an offense intentionally, one must confess it face-to-face once;
if committed through negligence, one must have a mind of regret.
These ten are all termed "aggregates" (khandha).
This is because all the precepts are gathered therein.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Question: [Why is this so?]
There is transgression of the precepts with a wholesome mind;
there is transgression of the precepts with a neutral mind.
Answer:
If there is a newly ordained bhikṣu who does not know the characteristics of the precepts,
and he personally pulls up the grass before a stūpa or the grass on a walking path,
or he himself repairs the walking path.
To personally gather flowers for offering is called an offense committed with a wholesome mind.
An unwholesome mind, however, acts intentionally despite knowing [the precept].
One with an indeterminate mind is one who does not intentionally transgress the precepts.
Question:
Is the wholesome mind of an Arhat indeterminate?
Answer:
When an Arhat violates the precepts, it is always with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
That is to say, he does not consciously reflect that there is more [food] and thus eats repeatedly.
One should not enter a village without having announced one's arrival.
One should not enter a settlement wearing the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
If one sleeps, one should sleep on a high bed placed upon a ground-litter.
While he was asleep, another person took a woman onto the bed;
having stayed for more than two nights with one who had not yet received full ordination,
he entered the lodging while already asleep.
Having awakened, he felt regret.
Such instances as these concern questions regarding the indeterminate mind.
The Buddha taught that one who is insane does not violate the precepts.
What constitutes madness? There are five causes and conditions by which one is called mad:
first, the loss of wealth;
second, the loss of kinsmen.
Third, the four great elements are in disharmony;
fourth, one is afflicted by non-human spirits;
fifth, it is the retribution for obstacles caused by past karma.
These are called the five kinds of insanity.
If one feigns an act of violating the precepts while knowing oneself to be a bhikṣu,
one incurs an offense according to the specific act.
One who is unaware does not commit an offense. How is it that one whose mind is distracted does not commit an offense? Answer:
There are five causes and conditions by which the mind becomes distracted:
namely, seeing non-human beings and becoming terrified, which distracts the mind.
Non-human beings seize one's vital essence;
the four great elements are in disharmony;
and there is retribution from past lives as well as being struck by non-human beings.
This is called "offense" and "non-offense.
As previously stated, regarding how one experiences pain and affliction yet does not violate the precepts,
there are likewise five causes and conditions.
First, provoked by wind;
second, provoked by cold;
third, provoked by heat.
Fourth, arising from a combination of factors;
fifth, arising at a specific time.
These are called the five types of offenses.
